families.Session: Starting a MAME session, asking what state it is in, finding its window, choosing a cpu and ending it.
families.Machine: What the emulated machine is made of, how the debugger holds each cpu, and what MAME writes to its logs.
families.Names: Look up a name or an address in your program's symbol table, and ask the knowledge base what a number is called.
families.Run: The tools that let the program run and stop it again.
families.Breakpoints: Breakpoints and watches the server saves by name and sets again in later sessions.
families.Read: Reading what the stopped program holds: memory, registers, code, and which of its screens is showing.
families.Screen: Seeing a board's graphics as data: the palette entry behind each pixel, tiles decoded from ROM or memory, and the draws a board makes.
families.Timeline: MAME's tools that load a project's graphics manifest and show, frame by frame, when a write happened and which code set a colour.
families.Scan: Finding the address of a value nobody has named yet.
families.Write: Changing the machine: memory, a register, a reset, and any line the debugger console takes.
families.Comments: Notes on addresses of the program, saved with the breakpoints and shown in the disassembly.
families.Lua: Pressing the board's inputs, running Lua inside MAME, and choosing whether the machine runs at real speed.
families.States: Saved states: the whole emulated machine written to a file, listed, and loaded back.
families.Captures: Saving the screen and the sound to files: a still, a series of frames, a video, a recording, and the list of them.
families.Files: Comparing pictures and recordings on disk, in numbers, with no machine running.
families.Sequences: Running several calls as one: a list of steps, an input with its check, and a session written as a replay script.
families.Project: Saving what a session learned into the repository's `.scry/` folder, after a review.

start.what: Start MAME on a system, stopped at the debugger, after checking that it runs the program your reference image holds.
start.ask: Start Gridlee in a window I can watch without losing my keyboard, with these symbols, checked against this image at 0xa000.
start.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org. The example session starts it for a person to watch, with seven symbols and a reference image of the program ROM at `0xa000`.
start.reads: The check passed, seven symbols are loaded and the machine is stopped at `0x0000f000` on frame 0. `kept` says the arguments were saved as a start profile, for `promote` to write into a repository.

arguments.system: The system to run, by MAME's short name. Required unless a start profile gives it.
arguments.rompath: The folders that hold the system's ROMs, separated by `;`. Required unless a start profile gives it.
arguments.reference_rom: A binary image of the program you expect to be running, which the machine's memory is compared with. Required unless a start profile gives it.
arguments.symbols: A symbol file, so an address can be given by name: a YAML file or the linker's five-column map. One path is the first cpu's; `{cpu: path}` gives one per cpu.
arguments.reference_addr: The address where 16 bytes of the machine are compared with the image: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, 0.
arguments.inipath: The folders MAME reads its `.ini` files from, separated by `;`. Left empty, MAME's own.
arguments.boot_seconds: How long to wait for MAME's debugger to answer, in seconds. Left out, 8.
arguments.shared: `true` when a person watches: a large window at real speed. Left out, a small window that runs unthrottled.
arguments.display: Which display the window opens on, by the operating system's index. Needs `shared=true`; left out, 0, the main display.
arguments.size: The window's size as `WIDTHxHEIGHT`, in the host's unit. Needs `shared=true`; left out, the largest whole multiple of the screen that fits the display.
arguments.background: `true` opens the window behind your other windows and leaves the keyboard focus where it is; `false` opens it in front. Left out, behind unless `shared`.
arguments.boot_lua: A Lua file MAME runs at boot, after the server's own script. It is a path, never Lua text.
arguments.env: Environment variables for MAME's own process, as `{name: value}`. They are there for what `boot_lua` reads.
arguments.bases: For a linker's map: the address each class other than CODE is based at, as `0x` text or an integer, or `rom`. With per-cpu `symbols`, `{cpu: {class: base}}`.
arguments.reference_base: The address of the image's first byte. Left out, 0.
arguments.stub_port: The TCP port of MAME's gdbstub, the remote-debugger connection this server uses. Left at 0, a free port is picked.
arguments.state_dir: The folder for saved states, `cfg/` and `nvram/`, which stays after `close`. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.throttle_from_frame: Runs unthrottled until this frame and at real speed from it on, with either kind of window. Left at 0, the speed follows `shared`.
arguments.types: A file of `name: format` lines, one per symbol whose value has a format. With per-cpu `symbols`, `{cpu: file}`.
arguments.cfg: A `.cfg` file the server installs as the system's own before it boots. Left empty, MAME runs on its defaults.
arguments.binary: The MAME to run: an executable, or a `.app` bundle holding one. Left empty, `MAME_BINARY`, else the `mame` on the PATH.
arguments.presence: Draws a border around the emulator's window while the session is open, brighter while a call runs the machine. `false` leaves it off.
arguments.overlay: Marks over the border, on by default: `calls` names each call, `keys` the fields held, `pause` a stopped machine, `record` a recording. `place` is `top`, `bottom` or `auto`.
arguments.view: What `snapshot` and `record` draw. Left empty, the emulated screen at its own size; else one of MAME's layout views, named by how its name begins.
arguments.profile: A start profile: a saved set of `start` arguments, by its name under `.scry/start/` or by a path. It fills only the arguments the call leaves out.
arguments.names: `false` leaves a reply's numbers bare, with no `names` field, no name in its summary and no note on a disassembled line.

returns.rom_check: `OK` when the 16 bytes read from the machine equal the image's. A start whose check fails is refused.
returns.window: With `shared`, where the window is. Its `front` is `true` when no other application's window covers its centre; it does not mean the window has the keyboard focus.
returns.profile: With a start profile: its `name`, its `file`, and `supplied`, the arguments it filled.
returns.kept: Says that this start's arguments were saved as a start profile for `promote`, the tool that writes one into your repository's `.scry/` folder.
returns.start_retries: Present when MAME had to be launched more than once: what each earlier attempt left.

refuses: A session is already open (`session_live`).
The 16 bytes differ from the image's; the session is closed (`readback_refused`).
`system`, `rompath` or `reference_rom` given neither by the call nor by a start profile, a path that is not absolute, or a folder where a file is expected (`bad_argument`).
A `reference_addr` outside the image, a `stub_port` that is not free, or a `cfg` MAME would not read (`bad_argument`).
Per-cpu `symbols`, `bases` or `types` naming a cpu the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
A class of a linker's map with no base, `bases` beside a YAML file, or a bad line in `types` (`bad_argument`).
A `state_dir` that is the server's own folder for the saved breakpoints file, directly or through a link: a session with a `state_dir` keeps its own (`bad_argument`).
`display` or `size` without `shared=true`, a `display` the host does not have, or a `size` larger than the display's usable area (`bad_argument`).
A `profile` that no `.scry/` folder searched holds; `searched` lists them (`bad_argument`).
A window that never appears on the display asked for. The session stays open for `window` or `close` (`window_not_visible`).
A MAME that exits or never answers during the boot (`session_broken`).
why: Before it answers, `start` reads 16 bytes of the machine at `reference_addr` and compares them with `reference_rom`. If they differ, MAME is not running the program your addresses describe. The session is then closed, because one left open would answer the next call about another program.

`shared` says whether a person watches. Without it MAME opens a small window, unthrottled and behind your other windows, which `window` cannot report. With it the window opens on `display`, in front and at real speed; add `background=true` to watch without losing the keyboard focus.

A start profile is a file of `start` arguments, `.scry/start/<name>.json` in a repository, so a session starts with `start(profile="<name>")`. The call's own arguments win and the profile fills the rest. The `.scry/` folder is looked for upwards from the server's working directory, then from `rompath` and `binary`.
why_more:
| you want | arguments | the window |
|---|---|---|
| Nobody watching | `shared=false`, the default | Small, unthrottled, behind. `window` refuses it as `no_channel`. |
| Somebody watching | `shared=true`, with `display` and `size` if wanted | On the display, in front, at real speed, confirmed in the host's window list. |
| Watching and keeping the keyboard focus | `shared=true`, `background=true` | The same, opened behind your other windows. |
**The window's size.**

A watched window is the largest whole multiple of the machine's first screen that fits the display's usable area. The window's frame counts; the menu bar, Dock and taskbar do not. MAME draws the picture at the view's aspect and scales it by whole pixels, so it is letterboxed where the view's shape is not the screen's.

`size` wins over that fit, in the host's unit: points on macOS, real pixels on Windows. One that does not fit is refused, naming the usable size. One that is not a whole multiple of the screen is scaled unevenly, and the `note` says so.
`start` waits until the host lists the window on that display. Do not select `-video none` yourself: on macOS it takes over the display.

`background` only chooses where the window opens. How the focus stays with you is the host's: on macOS the emulator starts as a background application, and on Windows no program may take the foreground while `start` launches. A click or ALT moves the focus as always.
**Fast-forward to a late scene.**

`throttle_from_frame=N` runs unthrottled to frame N, then at real speed, and logs `MAME_MCP throttled from frame N`. Waiting for that line with `log_wait` also restarts the span `close` measures `average_speed` over, so the speed is the real-speed part alone. It is fixed at launch; `throttle` switches the speed of an open session.
**The boot.**

- A MAME that exits while `start` waits ends the wait at once, and the refusal gives its exit code.
- One still alive when `boot_seconds` runs out is `session_broken`; `stdout_kept` is a saved copy of what it printed.
- A crash by a signal before the debugger answers, or a port another process took first, is launched again a few times. `start_retries` lists the attempts.
- An exit code (missing ROMs, an unknown system, a bad option) would come again, so it is refused at once.
- A MAME that dies after `start` answered is never launched again.
- An unknown `system` is refused in MAME's own words: after the launch, or before it on a `shared` start or with per-cpu `symbols`.
- A gdbstub that does not describe the board's first cpu is `no_channel`: that MAME build cannot serve the board.
- Another process listening on a `stub_port` you named is `host_failed`, naming its pid.
- `start` connects once, after MAME prints its debugger banner. A build that never prints it costs every start its whole `boot_seconds`.
**Symbols and files.**

- A symbol file belongs to one cpu, because each cpu runs its own program. With `{cpu: path}`, `bases` and `types` are per cpu too, and the single shape is refused.
- `symbols_total`, `symbols_typed`, `symbols_format` and `symbols_by_class` describe the first cpu's file; `symbols_by_cpu` counts each.
- `boot_lua` runs after the server's own boot script, so `boot_lua_path` is the combined script. One that calls `manager.machine:exit()` ends the machine under the session.
- With `state_dir` empty, saved states, `cfg/` and `nvram/` live in the temporary folder `scratch_dir` names. Nothing is written into your project either way.
- `cfg` is copied to where MAME reads it; your file is never touched. MAME reports a rejected `.cfg` on stderr only, so the server reads that and refuses the start.
- A `type:` line under a YAML symbol, or a `types` line, says what the symbol is, so a watch needs no `fmt`. A pointer's type names what it points at.
**What else the reply says.**

- `version` is the build's own `-version` line and `recommended_release` the MAME version this server is tested on. Another version starts with a `note`, never a refusal.
- `debugger.note`: the machine runs under the debugger, so a capture at a stop can land one frame from a reference capture an autoboot script took at the same frame count.
- `machine` holds counts only; `machine_map` has the rows. If MAME's `-listxml` fails, the start still works and the `note` says what is left empty.
- `frame_symbol` is the name the frame counter answers to; a board with no screen has none ([Run](run.md)).
- `flags`, `env`, `view`, `background`, `binary_origin`, `errorlog_path` and `stdout_path` say what the launch used, so a start can be told from another by its own reply.
- `presence` is `true` while the border is drawn. A failure drawing it never changes another reply: `presence`, here and in `status`, turns `available: false` with a `why`.
- `overlay` is there with the border on: the `layers` drawn, the `place` in effect, and in `lacking` why one is not. MAME has no pointer, so that layer is lacking.

status.what: Ask whether a session is open and what the machine is doing, without moving it.
status.ask: Is the emulator still up, and where is it stopped?
status.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), right after that start: the machine is stopped and nothing has run.
status.reads: Gridlee is up and stopped at `0x0000f000`. `in_debugger` is empty because no breakpoint or watch is set yet, and `cpu_tags` names the board's one cpu.

returns.last_stop: Where the machine last stopped: its `pc`, `cpu` and `cause`, and `since_s`, how long ago. Unavailable, with why, when there is no stop to report.
returns.pc: Where the machine stands now. Unavailable while it runs or once the session is broken; `last_stop.pc` is then the answer.
returns.stopped_on_its_own: Present when the machine had stopped and no call had reported it yet. `status` records that stop as the last one.
returns.broken: Present when the session can no longer be trusted, with the reason. The way out is `close`, then `start`.
returns.in_debugger: What MAME's debugger holds now: `breakpoints`, `watches` and `regpoints` (registerpoints, stops on a register condition), each by its `ref`, a symbol or an address, and its `cpu`.
returns.fingerprint: A hash of the system, the reference image and the symbol file. A breakpoint or watch saved under another one is not trusted; `fingerprints` has one per cpu.

why: `status` answers in every state: with no session, while the machine runs and once the session is broken. It is where you learn why another tool does not answer.
why_more:
- With no session the reply is `last_stop` and, when there is one to give, a `note`. After MAME exited under the session it is `exit_code` and a `note`.
- `debugger.note` says a capture at a stop can land one frame from an autoboot reference capture; `start` says why.
- `threads` is empty on a MAME without the gdbstub thread patch, which gives each cpu a debugger thread. `cpu_tags` only names the cpus; what each is doing is `cpu_info`'s.
- `console_pending` counts Lua lines sent and not yet run. `throttles_pending` lists speed switches asked and not yet applied (`tag`, `on`).
- `tallies_pending_removal` lists write counts waiting to be removed (`tally_id`, `call`); a row that leaves is a removal done.
- `presence` is `true` when the border is drawn, `false` when it was asked off, or the reason it is not drawn.
- `overlay` is there with the border on, as `start` gave it: the `layers` drawn, the `place` in effect and, in `lacking`, why a layer is not.
- `last_stop` also carries `stop_seq`, `frame` and `wall_at`. `frame_symbol` is the frame counter's name, as `start` found it.
- `cfg`, `stdout_path`, `errorlog_path`, `scratch_dir` and `state_dir` are the session's files, as `start` named them.
- `knowledge` counts the entries of the base the names come from (`served`) and those not served yet (`held_back`), whose numbers stay numbers.

window.what: Find where the session's window is on your displays and whether another window covers it, or bring it in front.
window.ask: Where is the emulator's window, and can I see it?
window.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), started with `shared=true` so that it has a window to report.
window.reads: The run hides the `window` block and the summary here, because where the window is differs on every host. `status` is `ok`: the host listed the window.

arguments.front: `true` brings the window in front of whatever covers it and reads the result back. Left out, the window is reported where it is and nothing moves.

returns.window: Where it is: `display`, `bounds`, `onscreen`, `fullscreen` and `front`. `front` is `true` when no other application's window covers its centre; it does not mean the window has the keyboard focus.
returns.size: Only when `start` named a `size`: what was `asked`, what is `seen`, and whether it `matches` within `tolerance_px`.

refuses: No session is open (`no_session`).
The session's emulator died (`session_broken`).
The session was started without `shared`, so there is no watched window to report (`no_channel`).
The window never appears, or with `front` is still covered after it was activated. `seen` says what the host listed (`window_not_visible`).
why: `front` answers one question: can a person see the picture? It is `true` when the window is on screen and no other application's window covers its centre. It is not the keyboard focus, which a window nothing covers can be without.

`window` answers at any time, a running machine included. Without `front` it moves nothing and reports the window wherever you put it. With `front`, a session started with `background=true` may stay behind, and the refusal names that as the likely cause.
A `size` given to `start` is checked here, at any moment, a start still stopped included, because MAME sizes its window when it creates it. The size the server chose by itself is never checked.
why_more:
- `compared` says which rectangle was measured: `client`, the area inside the frame, on Windows; `outer` on macOS, which has no client area, so a title bar's height is allowed.
- `height_free` is `true` when the emulator fits the height to the picture's aspect by itself, so only the width is checked. MAME does this on Windows.
- `display` is the operating system's index, and `fullscreen` is `true` when the window's bounds are the display's.
- On a `window_not_visible` refusal, `asked_display` is the display `start` asked for and `activation` what bringing it forward answered.

close.what: End the session and the emulator with it, and learn how it ended.
close.ask: We are done: close the emulator and tell me how it ended.
close.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), at the end of the example session, after it saved a screen map and a list of steps.
close.reads: MAME quit when asked, with exit code 0, and wrote its cfg. `draft` names three things the session saved that `promote` can still write into a repository's `.scry/` folder.

arguments.detail: `true` returns the last lines the emulator printed (`stdout_tail`, `errorlog_tail`) after a clean quit too. Left out, they come only when the end was not clean.

returns.closed: `true` when a session was ended; `false` when there was none to close.
returns.exit_code: The emulator's exit code. It is `available: false` with a `why` when no session was running or the killed process could not be collected.
returns.average_speed: The emulation speed over the last run `resume` opened, as `percent`. Absent when no such run was open.
returns.cfg: With a `cfg` at `start`: `installed_path`, and `changed`, whether MAME rewrote the installed copy.
returns.draft: The names of what the session saved and `promote` has not yet written into your repository's `.scry/` folder.

why: `close` asks MAME to quit through its console and kills it only when it has not gone within the grace period. MAME writes `cfg/` and `nvram/` on a clean exit only, and ignores SIGTERM. `ended_by` says which happened, since `closed: true` would say the same of every ending.

It is the one way out of every state: it works on a running machine and on a broken session, and with no session it answers `closed: false`. The session's temporary folder is deleted; a `state_dir` you named stays.

`session` describes the state after the close: `alive`, `running` and `altered` are `false`, as with no session. A doubt about what the session reported, a console error count or a speed switch that never applied, is still there, because it stays true of the answers you have.
why_more:
- `quit`: a clean exit. `cfg_written` says whether MAME wrote its cfg, and is unavailable when there was no cfg file to read.
- `exited`: it exited and wrote none.
- `killed`: killed after the grace period. `exit_code` is unavailable if the process is still not collected.
- `died`: it had already exited.
- `none`: there was no session.

- `average_speed` is the server's own measure, the debugger's emulated clock over the wall clock: MAME prints no speed line when it exits from the debugger.
- It holds `percent` and the two deltas, or `available: false` with a `why`.
- Lua lines still waiting in the console are run before the quit, because one left there can crash MAME on its way out. `console_pending_before` and `console_drained` count them.
- The `note` names the lines that could not be run, so a bad exit code has its likely cause beside it.
- `cfg` is unavailable when no cfg was given, and `changed` says so when the copy could not be read back.
- When the last lines are left out, `omitted` names them and `how` says what brings them.
- On a broken session `close` asks MAME nothing: no drain, no speed read and no `quit`, only the kill.
- The last lines are read before the temporary folder is deleted, so a MAME that died still gives its last words in `stdout_tail` and `errorlog_tail`.

cpu_focus.what: Choose which cpu MAME's debugger shows, the one every call that names no `cpu` acts on.
cpu_focus.ask: Show me the main cpu in the debugger.
cpu_focus.on: This needs a board with more than one cpu, which neither free ROM has. The reply shown comes from a test program that is not distributed.
cpu_focus.reads: The main cpu was already the visible one. `via` `stub` and `machine_ran` `false` say nothing ran, and `unchanged` lists both cpus: their registers read the same before and after.

arguments.cpu: The cpu to show, by its tag in either spelling: `subcpu` or `:subcpu`. `machine_map` lists the tags.

returns.cpu: The cpu the debugger shows after the call, read back from its `cpulist`.
returns.via: `stub` when the gdbstub switched it, which runs nothing; `console` when the debugger's `focus` command did.
returns.machine_ran: `true` when the machine ran to make the switch. The reply then also describes the stop it reached.
returns.unchanged: With `stub`: the cpus whose registers read the same before and after, which is the evidence that nothing ran.
returns.ignored: With `console`: the cpus the debugger now ignores.

refuses: The machine is running (`not_stopped`).
A cpu the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
With the gdbstub thread patch, a cpu the debugger ignores (`bad_argument`).
The cpu read back afterwards is not the one asked for (`readback_refused`).
Without the patch, the run the console started reached no stop that was read (`not_settled`).
why: MAME's debugger acts on one cpu at a time, the visible one, and every stop makes the cpu that stopped visible. A call that names a `cpu` acts on that cpu and leaves the visible one alone, so `cpu_focus` is the call that moves it. [REFERENCE.md, The session](../../REFERENCE.md#the-session) has the whole rule.

On a MAME built with the gdbstub thread patch, which gives each cpu its own debugger thread, nothing runs. The reply shows it: `machine_ran: false`, the `frame`, and `unchanged`. Without the patch the debugger's `focus` command ignores every other cpu, and the machine may run until the chosen cpu executes.
why_more: `unread` names a cpu whose registers the gdbstub would not give, so it is never counted as unchanged.

rom_check.what: Check again that the machine runs the program your image holds, at any address and on any cpu.
rom_check.ask: Check again that the ROM at 0xa000 is still the image I gave you.
rom_check.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), stopped, with the reference image `start` was given.
rom_check.reads: The 16 bytes read from the machine equal the image's, and a second read gave the same bytes (`deterministic`). `cpu` names the cpu that was read.

arguments.reference_rom: The binary image to compare the machine's memory with.
arguments.reference_addr: The address where 16 bytes of the machine are compared with the image: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, 0.
arguments.reference_base: The address of the image's first byte. Left out, 0.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory is read. Left empty, the one the debugger shows.

returns.rom_check: `OK`: the 16 bytes read from the machine equal the image's.
returns.deterministic: `true` when reading the same address again gives the same bytes.
returns.query_s: How long one read through the debugger takes, in seconds.

refuses: The machine is running (`not_stopped`).
The bytes differ. The refusal names the cpu that was read, and the session stays open (`readback_refused`).
On a MAME without the gdbstub thread patch, which gives each cpu its own debugger thread, a cpu other than the first (`bad_argument`).
why: `start` makes this check once, with the image and address it was given. `rom_check` takes its arguments again on every call, so you can point it at another address, image or cpu. `state_write(method="load")` repeats `start`'s own check.

Name `cpu` once a stop has made another cpu the visible one, because an image is one cpu's program. The check is about the running machine, never about the MAME build. The second read is for `deterministic`, and `query_s` is what one read costs.
why_more: A MAME without the gdbstub thread patch reads its first cpu only, whatever the debugger shows.

cpu_info.what: List each cpu as the debugger sees it: visible, ignored or suspended, its program counter, and the breakpoints and watches set on it.
cpu_info.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset, right after `start`.
cpu_info.ask: Which cpus does this machine have, and which one is the debugger showing?
cpu_info.reads: Gridlee has one cpu, `:maincpu`. It is the `visible` one, which a call that names no cpu acts on; it sits at `0xf000` and nothing is set on it yet.

arguments.cpu: The tag of one cpu: only its row comes back and only its `pc` is read. Left empty, every cpu is listed.

returns.cpus: One row per cpu: its tag `cpu`, `visible`, `ignored`, `suspended`, its program counter `pc`, and `declarations`, the count of what is set on it.
returns.cpu: The full tag of the cpu you named; with none named, an object that says so.

refuses: A tag that names no cpu; the message lists the tags there are (`unknown_ref`).
A call with no session open (`no_session`).
A session that broke and has to be closed (`session_broken`).
why: Answering runs nothing and makes no cpu visible: the flags come from the debugger's own listings and each `pc` is read as a register. `visible` marks the cpu that a call naming none acts on, and a stop moves it. `ignored` means breakpoints and watches on that cpu have no effect.

A `pc` is unavailable, with the reason, while the program runs, and for every cpu but the first where MAME's gdbstub serves one cpu. A cpu the board itself holds in reset or halted shows nowhere: telling would mean moving the machine.
why_more:
- `declarations` counts `breakpoints`, `watches` and `regpoints`, armed or not. A regpoint is MAME's registerpoint, a stop on a condition over registers.
- A watch on an io port counts; one on a debugger expression belongs to no cpu and is not counted.
- `suspended` is the debugger's own `suspend`.
- Rows follow the debugger's `cpulist`, then any other cpu a saved breakpoint or watch names; of such a cpu only the counts are read.

machine_map.what: Get the layout of the machine: its cpus and their address spaces, the address map, memory regions and shares, screens and ROM files.
machine_map.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset, right after `start`.
machine_map.ask: What is this board made of: its cpu, its ROMs, its RAM, its screen?
machine_map.reads: `regions` are the ROMs MAME loaded and `shares` the blocks of RAM the board's devices share, each with its size in bytes. The sprite RAM is 2048 bytes.

arguments.cpu: The tag of one cpu, to narrow `cpus`, `spaces`, `address_map` and `symbol_coverage` to it. Left empty, every cpu's rows come back.
arguments.sections: Which sections to read. Left out, all of them but `rom_files`.
arguments.dest: A file to write every row of the sections read, as JSON: an absolute or `~` path that does not exist yet. Left empty, no file is written.

returns.cpus: One row per cpu: its tag `cpu`, MAME's short name `type`, `name`, `clock_hz` and the names of its `spaces`.
returns.address_map: One row per entry of a cpu's memory map: `cpu`, `space`, `index`, `start`, `end`, and the `share` or `region` behind it.
returns.sources: For each section, where its rows came from: `live` (the running machine), `-listxml` (MAME's own description of it) or `symbols` (your symbol table).
returns.counts: How many rows each section has in full, so a list cut short shows.
returns.truncated: `true` when a section had more than 400 rows and its list was cut; `dest` gets them all.
returns.path: With `dest`, the file that was written.

refuses: An empty `sections`, a name that is no section, or a `dest` that already exists (`bad_argument`).
A tag that names no cpu; the message lists the ones the machine has (`unknown_ref`).
A call with no session open (`no_session`).
A session that broke and has to be closed (`session_broken`).
why: The map is read once, while `start` boots the machine, so asking costs nothing and it answers while the program runs. It is the machine as `start` found it: nothing reads it again, even after the emulator has died.

Two sources fill it, because neither has everything. MAME's `-listxml`, run on this session's own binary, alone knows a clock, a screen's rotation and a ROM file's checksums. The running machine alone knows the shares, the region sizes, the address map and a cpu's `type`.
Where the two disagree the field carries the running machine's value, and `note` names both. A field neither source has is absent, never null or guessed.
why_more: The address map covers the devices that execute, the ones MAME gives a debugger. It is the map as wired: a banked range answers for whichever bank is selected at the time.

- `spaces`: `cpu`, `space`, `data_width_bits`, `endianness`, `entries`, `address_mask`.
- `address_map`: also `region_offset` beside a `region`, and the entry's own `mirror` and `address_mask` when not zero. A `share` or `region` carries the tag `shares` and `regions` list it under.
- `regions` and `shares`: `tag`, `size`, `bytewidth`, `endianness`.
- `screens`: `tag`, `width`, `height`, `refresh_hz`, `rotation`, `type`.
- `rom_files`: `name`, `size`, `crc`, `sha1`, `dump_status`, `region`, `offset`. It is left out by default because it answers a ROM audit, not a debugging question.
- `symbol_coverage`: one row per class of each cpu's symbol table, with `class`, `cpu`, `span` (`from`, `length`), `symbols` and `base`. It is empty when the table has no classes.
- `cpu` leaves the regions, shares, screens and ROM files whole: they are the board's, and a shorter list would say the other cpu's ROMs do not exist.
- When `-listxml` fails, `rom_files`, the clocks and the rotation are empty and `note` quotes why.
- `frame_symbol` names the machine's frame counter, unavailable on a board with none. `omitted` and `how` name the sections left out and how to ask for them.

log.what: Read the newest log lines that match a pattern: from MAME's own log, from the process's output, or from both.
log.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, after one coin has been dropped.
log.ask: What has MAME logged about the coin counter?
log.reads: Three lines of MAME's own log match, oldest first: the driver reports the coin counter off, then on for the coin, then off again.

arguments.pattern: A regular expression each line is searched for. It is never empty: `.` matches every line.
arguments.channel: Which log to read. `emulator` is MAME's `error.log`, `process` its stdout and stderr, `all` both with each line tagged `[emulator] ` or `[process] `.
arguments.limit: How many of the newest matching lines to return: 1 to 400. Left out, 40.
arguments.labels: `true` adds `labels`: the lines returned, counted by their first word. Left out, no count.
arguments.since_mark: A byte position in the log: only lines written after it are read. Left out or 0, the whole log is read.

returns.lines: The newest `limit` matching lines, oldest first.
returns.lines_total: How many lines matched in all, not how many came back.
returns.truncated: `true` when more matched than came back.
returns.counts: On `all`, how many lines matched in each of the two logs.
returns.labels: With `labels=true`, the returned lines counted by their first word: a quick view of who is writing.

refuses: An empty pattern, or one that is not a regular expression (`bad_argument`).
A `limit` outside 1 to 400 (`bad_argument`).
`channel` `guest`: an arcade board has no log written by the program itself (`bad_argument`).
A `since_mark` with `all`, or one past the end of the log (`bad_argument`).
A log MAME has written nothing to yet (`no_channel`).
why: A driver can fill the log fast, so the pattern and the limit are how a line is found. Pass a pattern that narrows: `.` is the last resort, and `labels` shows at a glance who is writing.
`emulator` is what MAME's core and the drivers write with `logerror`. `process` is where MAME's own error messages, its `-verbose` output and a driver's counters go.
`since_mark` takes the `mark` that a state load, or the log part of a stop's reply, gives for that log. It is a position in one file, so `all`, which reads two, takes none.

log_wait.what: Wait until a log line matches a pattern, or get the line at once when the log already has it.
log_wait.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, after turning the throttle off and letting the game run five seconds.
log_wait.ask: Check MAME's log for the line that says the throttle went off.
log_wait.reads: `TARGET` means a line matched, and `already` that the log held it before the call, so nothing was waited for. The line is the one MAME wrote when the throttle went off.

arguments.pattern: A regular expression each line is searched for. It is never empty: `.` matches every line.
arguments.channel: Which log to wait on: `emulator`, `process` or `all`, as in [`log`](#log).
arguments.seconds: How long to wait at most, in seconds, up to 600. Left out, 30.
arguments.since_mark: A byte position in the log: only lines written after it count, the ones already there included. Left out or 0, the whole log counts.

returns.verdict: `TARGET` when a line matched, `TIMEOUT` when the time ran out with none; `note` then says what was read.
returns.line: The first line that matched; for the newest one, use `log`.
returns.already: `true` when the log held the line before the call, so nothing was waited for.
returns.waited_s: Seconds spent waiting; 0 when the line was already there.
returns.arrived_during: How many lines were written during the wait, whether or not they matched.
returns.lines_examined: How many lines were read in all: those the log held and those that came during the wait.

refuses: A machine stopped at the debugger, or one that stops during the wait, while the log lacks the line: a stopped machine logs nothing (`wait_stopped`).
An emulator that exits during the wait (`session_broken`).
`seconds` out of range, an empty or malformed pattern, or a `since_mark` past the end of the log (`bad_argument`).
why: The log is read before any waiting, so a line written before the call is found at once, where a tool that only waited would report that it never came. `already` marks such a line.

A `TIMEOUT` says what it read. `arrived_during` counts the lines written during the wait and `lines_examined` every line read, so a program that wrote nothing is told apart from one whose lines did not match.
A stop during the wait is refused like a machine already stopped, after one last read of the log. After a `TIMEOUT` the program still runs. Progress is reported while it waits.
why_more: `lines_before` counts the lines read before the match and `lines_total` the matches in that read.

symbols_find.what: Find a symbol's address by its name, or find which symbol an address falls in.
symbols_find.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, started with the symbol file of the reference's own run, `docs/reference/tour/gridlee-symbols.yaml`.
symbols_find.ask: Which symbols start with "cred", and where are they?
symbols_find.reads: No symbol is named `cred`, so the two that start with it are listed: the credits and their BCD copy, one byte apart. `memory` says both sit in RAM.

arguments.name: The symbol to look up, case ignored. An exact match wins; with none, every symbol that starts with it is listed, by address.
arguments.linear: An address as the running program uses it, as `disassemble` shows it. The reply is the nearest symbol at or below it.
arguments.limit: How many symbols a name lookup lists: 1 to 50. Left out, 10.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose table is read. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.symbols: By name: the first `limit` matches, each with its `name` as the file spells it, its `addr` and its `memory`.
returns.symbols_total: By name: how many symbols matched.
returns.truncated: By name: `true` when more matched than `symbols` lists.
returns.name: By address: the nearest symbol at or below the address, with its own `addr`.
returns.delta: By address: how many bytes the address is past that symbol's start.
returns.memory: What kind of memory the symbol sits in: `ram`, `rom`, `latch`, `handlers`, `unmapped` or `unknown`.

refuses: Both `name` and `linear`, or neither: one question per call (`bad_argument`).
A session started with no symbol file for that cpu (`no_channel`).
An address below every symbol of the table (`unknown_ref`).
why: `memory` tells you, before you set one, that a watch for changes on the ROM copy of a variable can never fire. It costs the debugger's `map` command one question per symbol, hence the limit of 50.
The table is the server's own copy, not read from the machine, so the lookup answers while the program runs. While it runs `memory` is `unknown`, and `note` says why.

`linear` is a run-time address, after `start`'s `bases` moved the data to where the board keeps it. A linker map's column is before that, and finds a plausible symbol with an absurd `delta`. `delta` is a distance past the symbol's start because the table holds no sizes.
why_more:
| `memory` | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ram` | Read and written as plain memory: a watch for changes fires. |
| `rom` | Never written: code, or the ROM copy of a variable. |
| `latch` | Written through a handler, read nowhere: `read_memory` answers zeros; `read_block` reads it when the map entry keeps a share. |
| `handlers` | Read and written through handlers: readable, not plain memory. |
| `unmapped` | Nothing answers there. |
| `unknown` | The program is running, or `map` named no side. |

run_to.what: Run until the program reaches an address, or a screen of the screen map, and stop there.
run_to.ask: Run until the game counts the coin I dropped, and check that its frame-wait loop keeps running meanwhile.
run_to.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, started with the names in [gridlee-symbols.yaml](tour/gridlee-symbols.yaml) and stopped right after a coin is dropped.
run_to.reads: The run reached `count_coin`, which is what `TARGET` says. The control `wait_frame` ran once on the way, so breakpoints were firing.

arguments.ref: The address to stop at: a `0x` address or a symbol. Give this or `screen`, never both.
arguments.control: An address known to run often, counted beside the target, so that "the target never ran" can be told from "nothing ran". Required with `ref` or an anchored `screen`.
arguments.screen: A screen of the loaded screen map, the file naming a program's screens. With an `anchor`, an address the map gives it, the run goes there; without, frame by frame.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the stop, in real seconds, before the server interrupts the machine. Left out, 30.
arguments.disarm_watches: `true` takes your watches off for this run, so none of them stops it, and sets them again at the end.
arguments.condition: Stop at the target only when this expression holds, in the debugger's own grammar with bare numbers read as hex: `w@DemoLen==0x25`.
arguments.cpu: The cpu the target and the control are set on. Left empty, the visible one.

returns.verdict: How the run ended: `TARGET`, the target was reached; `TIMEOUT`, the wait gave up; `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch nobody targeted stopped it first.
returns.control_hits: How many times the controls ran during the run. A `TARGET` is `ok` even with none.
returns.controls: One row per control counted on the target's cpu: its `ref`, its `cpu` and `hits_in_run`. It comes with a run to a `ref` or an anchor.
returns.target_disarmed: Whether the run's own breakpoint at the target was removed. It comes only when it was not, or when the interrupt at the time limit was answered late or never.
returns.frames: How many frames a run to a screen with no `anchor` took.
returns.screen: After a run to a screen: its `screen`, `layer` and `mode`, and `judged`, whether the map checked the screen there.

refuses: A `ref`, a `control` or a `screen` that the symbol table or the screen map does not name (`unknown_ref`).
No `control` with a `ref` or an anchored screen, or a `control` or `disarm_watches` with a screen that has no anchor (`bad_argument`).
A target at a control's address, or at an address where one of your breakpoints already stops (`bad_argument`).
A `condition` too long for one console command; the reply gives `command_chars` and `limit_chars` (`bad_argument`).
A target MAME's console accepted and does not list, found before the machine moves (`readback_refused`).
A `TIMEOUT` during which no control ran: nothing was learned about the target (`control_silent`).
Another stop before any control ran (`cut_by_other_stop`).
An interrupt at the time limit that got no answer: the machine may still be running, so call `stop` (`not_settled`).
A screen map that no longer matches the screen at its anchor (`stale_map`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: Several different mistakes leave a MAME breakpoint silent, and each looks exactly like "that routine is never called". The control counting beside the target tells them apart. A `TIMEOUT` with no control hit is refused, because it cannot tell a wrong address from a right one that runs less often than assumed.

The target is a temporary breakpoint of the run's own, removed when the run ends. It cannot share an address with a breakpoint you set, since a stop there could not be told from the target's. A stop at the target's address is `TARGET` only when it is the target cpu's.
`disarm_watches` is for a watch on a byte written every frame, which would otherwise stop every later run.
why_more: A control on another cpu runs another program, and runs even while the target's cpu is held in reset, so it cannot say that cpu ran. Naming one is `unknown_ref`, with `control_on` and the `breakpoint_at(..., cpu=)` call that fixes it.

Both breakpoints are read back from MAME's list before the machine moves. A target the console took and does not list would otherwise come back `TIMEOUT` beside a control that ran. One listed without its `condition` is removed first, or every later run would stop there.

When the time limit passes the server interrupts the machine. An interrupt answered late is a `TIMEOUT` whose `cause` says "answered late". One never answered is `not_settled` with no `cause`: call `stop`, and if `stop` fails as well, `close` then `start`.

A removal MAME refuses after the stop does not undo the stop. The reply keeps its readings with `target_disarmed: false`, and `note` names the `debug("bpclear 0x<row>")` that removes the breakpoint. `declaration_clear` cannot, because the target was never one of yours.

- `control_silent` still carries the stop's readings, a `note`, and `control_dasm`: the code at each control (`ref`, `cpu`, `dasm`).
- `disarmed_watches` lists the watches taken off and `not_rearmed` those not set again, by `ref` and `cpu`. After `session_broken` they stay off.

run_for.what: Run for a number of frames or milliseconds of emulated time and come back stopped.
run_for.ask: Let the game run for five seconds of its own time, then stop.
run_for.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, right after `start`.
run_for.reads: `ELAPSED` says the five seconds ran out as asked. The frame counter went from 0 to 295, the emulated clock reads a little over 5 seconds, and the cpu spent 6250000 cycles.

arguments.milliseconds: How much emulated time to run, in milliseconds. Give this or `frames`, never both.
arguments.frames: How many frames to run, counted on MAME's frame counter. Give this or `milliseconds`, never both.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the run to end, in real seconds. Left out, 30.
arguments.disarm_watches: `true` takes your watches off for this run, so none of them stops it, and sets them again at the end.

returns.verdict: How the run ended: `ELAPSED`, the frames or time asked for ran out, as asked; `TIMEOUT`, the wait gave up; `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch stopped it first.
returns.frame_after: The frame counter after the run; `frame_before` is the one before. Unavailable, with why, on a board with no frame counter.
returns.emulated_after_s: The emulated clock after the run, in seconds; `emulated_before_s` is the one before.
returns.cycles: The cpu cycles the run took, for what was asked and nothing else. Unavailable, with why, when they cannot be counted.
returns.polls: By frames: how many single-frame runs were sent. One more than `frames` means the run began in the middle of a frame.
returns.reads: By milliseconds: how many times the counter was read until it stood still.

refuses: Both `milliseconds` and `frames`, or neither (`bad_argument`).
`frames` on a board with no frame counter: run it by `milliseconds` (`no_channel`).
A run during which the counter did not move (`no_progress`).
A counter that went backwards: something put the machine back during the run (`frames_went_backwards`).
A counter or a clock still moving at the time limit: the machine may still be running, so call `stop` (`not_settled`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: A run by frames counts MAME's frame counter itself, so a capture can be taken again at the same frame; N milliseconds is not N frames. A run is `ELAPSED` only once several readings spaced apart agree the machine has stopped: one handed back still running is the worst state for a session.

By frames the run goes through the first cpu: MAME keeps "a vblank happened", the end of a frame's drawing, as one flag. The first cpu to run after it consumes the flag, so only that cpu stops there. `note` says when that cpu had to be made visible.

`cycles` spans what was asked for. A run that starts in the middle of a frame first spends one single-frame run reaching the vblank it is inside. That one moves no counter, and `polls` is how it shows.
why_more: `cycles` is unavailable on the first run after a load, a rewind or a reset typed through `debug`. MAME's debugger refreshes its cycle counter only when the cpu executes, so the span would be off by the distance between the two states. It is also unavailable when the run was counted on one cpu and stopped on another.

A board with no screen device has no frame counter and is run by `milliseconds`. MAME registers `frame` on a machine with one screen device and `frame0`, `frame1` and so on with several, where the first one is used. `start` asks MAME and reports the name as `frame_symbol`.

A vector board has a display and no screen device, so the screens `machine_map` lists are no guide. There a stop's `frame` is unavailable and the emulated clock confirms the stop. An expression MAME's console refuses there is `no_channel`: an answer about the machine, not a broken session.

- A MAME without one debugger thread per cpu cannot change the visible cpu without running, so it refuses `frames` while another cpu is visible.
- `no_progress` by frames leaves the machine running until `stop` and carries no stop readings. By milliseconds it carries them.
- After `not_settled`, call `stop`. If `stop` fails as well, `close` then `start`.
- The call reports progress to the client while it waits.
- A run started while a registerpoint's condition still holds stops one instruction later as `OTHER_STOP`, never `no_progress`.
- A single-frame run MAME refused, or whose landing was not read, may still have been taken: the session is marked running and the call is `not_settled`.

step.what: Execute a few instructions of one cpu, going into calls or over them.
step.ask: Execute one instruction and show me where the cpu is now.
step.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at `count_coin`, where the `run_to` example above ends.
step.reads: One instruction ran, going into any call, and the main cpu is now at `0xb586`, in frame 552. The whole reply shows the instruction that runs next.

head: mode
what it does
rows: Executes one instruction, and enters a call.
Runs a call to its return as one step.

arguments.count: How many instructions to execute. Left out, one.
arguments.cpu: The cpu to step, made visible first. Left empty, the visible one.

returns.instructions_completed: How many instructions ran. Fewer than `count` when a stop on another cpu ended the steps, which `note` says.
returns.others: Every other cpu's program counter `before` and `after` the steps, with its register's name in `reg`. Only on a MAME built with one debugger thread per cpu.

refuses: A named `cpu` on a MAME that cannot show another cpu without running it (`bad_argument`).
A step whose stop did not come in time: the machine may still be running, so call `stop` (`not_settled`).
An answer that is not a stop where one was due, a failed connection, or an `over` MAME did not answer in time (`session_broken`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: Each step is confirmed on the program counter, because MAME's console answers an `over` while the machine is still running to the call's return.
The largest `count` is what keeps the longest run of `over` steps inside the time limit every wait has. Past it the tool to use is `run_to` or `run_for`.

Naming a `cpu` makes it the visible one first, which runs nothing, and `others` shows what the rest did meanwhile. That needs a MAME built with one debugger thread per cpu: without it another cpu cannot be shown without running, so naming one is refused.
why_more: An `over` still moving at its time limit is interrupted, and whether the call would have returned is not seen. An `over` MAME refused may still have been taken, so the session is marked as running and `stop` brings it back; if `stop` fails as well, `close` then `start`.
An `into` whose stop is late still has that stop to come, and `stop` waits for it. The `not_settled` reply carries `mode` and `instructions_completed`.

An `into` that reads anything else in a stop's place, a failed connection, or an `over` the console did not answer in time is `session_broken`. That stays set until `close`, because the late answer would otherwise be read as the next request's.

resume.what: Let the machine run, either with no deadline or waiting a while for it to stop.
resume.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped right after a reset.
resume.reads: With no `seconds` the call returns at once and the game keeps running. The `stop` after it interrupted the machine: the session's stop number 62.

arguments.seconds: How long to wait for a stop, in real seconds. Left at 0, the call returns at once and the machine keeps running.

returns.verdict: With `seconds`: `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch stopped the machine, and the stop's readings follow; `TIMEOUT`, nothing did, and it is left running with a `note`.
returns.waited_s: With `seconds`: how long the call waited.
returns.average_speed: With a stop: how fast the machine ran, as `percent` of real time, over `emulated_s` and `wall_s`.

refuses: A machine that is already running (`not_stopped`).
An answer that is not a stop where one was due, a resume that could not be sent, or a stop that could not be read (`session_broken`).
why: While the machine runs, the tools that read it refuse. Each refusal names `last_stop`, the stop the machine was last seen at, and `answers_while_running`, the tools that still answer.
A `resume` with `seconds` reports progress while it waits. After `session_broken` the way out is `close`, then `start`.

stop.what: Stop a running machine where it is and read where it stopped.
stop.ask: Stop the game where it is.
stop.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, running after a `resume`.
stop.reads: `interrupted: true` means this call stopped the machine. It is the session's stop number 62, on the main cpu; where it lands differs from run to run.

returns.interrupted: `true` when this call stopped the machine, with the stop's readings. `false` when it was already stopped, with a `note`.
returns.average_speed: How fast the machine ran since it was resumed: `percent` of real time, over `emulated_s` and `wall_s`.

refuses: An interrupt the machine did not answer, or a frame counter that still moves: the machine stays marked as running, so ask again (`not_settled`).
An interrupt answered by something that is not a stop, a failed connection, or a stop that could not be read (`session_broken`).
why: `stop` is the way back from any run that ended without knowing whether the machine stopped. A run by frames refused as `no_progress` is brought back here: the interrupt is what confirms the stop.
Nothing counts the attempts. If `stop` fails as well, `close` then `start`.
why_more: `not_settled` also covers a run started from MAME's console, through `debug`, whose frame counter still moves.

trace.what: Run for a number of frames or milliseconds and get every address one cpu executed, grouped by symbol.
trace.ask: Trace the next two frames and tell me which routines the game runs.
trace.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, started with the names in [gridlee-symbols.yaml](tour/gridlee-symbols.yaml) and stopped about a second into a new game.
trace.reads: In two frames, 628 to 630, the main cpu ran through 192 distinct addresses under 4 symbols, and the log is 19627 bytes. `trace`, in the whole reply, lists each symbol.

arguments.milliseconds: The window to trace, in milliseconds of emulated time. Give this or `frames`, never both.
arguments.frames: The window to trace, in frames. Give this or `milliseconds`, never both.
arguments.dest: Where MAME writes the trace: an absolute path to a new file. Left empty, a file in the session's temporary folder.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the run to end, in real seconds. Left out, 60.
arguments.cpu: The cpu to trace. Left empty, the visible one.
arguments.noloop: `true` logs every instruction, so the counts are exact and the largest window is shorter. Left out, MAME condenses loops and only the list of addresses is exact.

returns.trace: The result: `path` to MAME's log, `set_path` to the list of addresses, `instructions`, `addresses`, `unplaced` (addresses no symbol covers) and `symbols`.
returns.verdict: How the run ended, as in `run_for`: `ELAPSED`, the window ran out as asked; `TIMEOUT`, the wait gave up; `OTHER_STOP`, a breakpoint or a watch stopped it first.
returns.frame_after: The frame counter after the run, with `frame_before`, the clock and `cycles` as `run_for` returns them.

refuses: A `dest` that exists already, or whose list file `<name>-<extension>-set.jsonl` does (`bad_argument`).
A cpu with no disassembler, since the tracer disassembles every line it writes (`no_channel`).
A trace with no instruction line: the cpu executed nothing or the tracer recorded nothing, and the two look alike (`readback_refused`).
A tracer that could not be shown closed, with `trace.closed: false` (`readback_refused`).
A file MAME could not open (`host_failed`).
why: The tracer is armed and closed inside one call, because one left armed keeps writing on the next run of a client that forgot it. Arming replaces a trace typed through `debug` on that cpu. The limits on the window keep one call's output small; a longer window is consecutive calls.

MAME's tracer logs an address when the cpu reaches it, before executing it. So the address a stopped cpu is waiting at is missing from a trace armed there, and the address the run ends at is logged although never executed. Both are corrected, and `note` says which applied.

By default the tracer condenses loops: it keeps the last addresses and skips one it has seen twice among them. The list of addresses survives that, because an address is logged before it is skipped. The counts do not, so `instructions` is exact only under `noloop`.
why_more:
| in `trace` | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `path`, `bytes` | MAME's own log and its size |
| `set_path` | a file with one JSON line per executed address, ascending: `addr`, `symbol` when one covers it, `count` under `noloop` |
| `instructions`, `addresses`, `unplaced` | instructions logged, distinct addresses, addresses no symbol covers |
| `symbols` | the first rows, by address: `symbol`, `addr`, `addresses`, `first`, `last`, and `instructions` under `noloop` |
| `symbols_total`, `truncated` | how many symbols ran, and whether `symbols` leaves some out |
| `cpu`, `noloop`, `note` | the cpu traced, whether loops were kept whole, and the corrections applied |
| `closed` | on a refusal: whether the tracer was closed |

The tracer cannot see a cpu the debugger ignores, a cpu waiting on its own, or a stretch that runs with a save or a load pending. MAME calls no instruction hook for them. A cpu that pauses in the middle of an instruction, as MAME's 68000 does, finishes it after the window, unlogged.

When the tracer cannot be shown closed, the way out is `stop`, then `debug("trace off,<cpu>")`. If `stop` fails, `close` then `start`, since closing MAME closes the file. A run that ends `INVALID` carries `trace` with `path`, `bytes` and `closed`, and no list file.
One address can go missing from a condensed trace: address 0, when it runs among the first instructions, because the tracer's history starts as zeros.
The server never watches a run with no end: `trace` covers one bounded window. A count across an open-ended run is a job for a tracer you write in Lua and run with `lua`.

screen_wait.what: Run until the screen shows a mapped screen, a black palette or a change of screen, and stop there.
screen_wait.ask: Run until the level card is on screen.
screen_wait.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, with a screen map that names its level card, stopped right after START is pressed with two credits.
screen_wait.reads: The map's `level_card` screen was not up at the call, which is `already: false`. It came up 13 frames later, and the machine stopped there.

arguments.text: Not available here: MAME gives the screen as pixels, so waiting for text is refused. Map the screen with `screen_map_write` and wait on `screen`.
arguments.screen: Wait until this screen of the loaded screen map, the file naming a program's screens, is the one shown.
arguments.palette: `black` waits until every palette entry is black, which is how a fade ends.
arguments.changed: `true` waits until the screen map names a different screen from the one it named at the start. A frame it cannot name counts as in between.
arguments.every: How many frames to run between two looks at the screen. Left at 0, every frame; a screen shown for fewer frames than this can be missed.
arguments.on_breakpoint: Look at the screen only at the end of a frame in which this breakpoint fired: the `ref` of a `stop` breakpoint you set.
arguments.on_watch: The same for a watch: the `ref` of a `change` watch you set.
arguments.condition: Counts only the firings where this holds. Up to four terms joined by `&&`, each a register or a memory read (`b@ref`, `w@ref`, `d@ref`) compared with a hex value.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose breakpoint or watch `on_breakpoint` and `on_watch` name. Left empty, the visible one.
arguments.seconds: How long to keep looking, in real seconds, counted from the first look. Left out, 30.

returns.verdict: `TARGET` when what you waited for is on screen. `TIMEOUT` when the wait gave up, with a `note` and the machine stopped.
returns.already: `true` when it was on screen at the call, so the machine did not move.
returns.predicate: Which of `screen`, `palette` or `changed` was waited on.
returns.polls: How many frames ran, also given as `frames`; `sampled_every` repeats `every`.
returns.screen: The screen found, as `name` and `layer`. With `changed`, `started_on` is the screen it replaced.
returns.firings: With `on_breakpoint` or `on_watch`: how many times it fired. `frames_examined` counts the frames looked at after a firing.

refuses: None or several of `screen`, `palette` and `changed` (`bad_argument`).
`text`, or a palette that cannot be read at a stop (`no_channel`).
A screen the map does not name, or a breakpoint or watch you did not set (`unknown_ref`).
`changed` with no screen map loaded (`needs_call`).
A breakpoint or watch that never fired within `seconds`: no screen was looked at (`never_fired`).
A stop nobody asked for that ends the wait early; its `cause` and the stop's readings come with it (`wait_stopped`).
why: The server looks at the screen itself, at a stop at the end of a frame. MAME's own frame notifier is not used: it reads the screen a frame late and sometimes in the middle of a draw.

Without `on_breakpoint` or `on_watch` the wait looks every frame, or every `every` frames, which is how a screen that is slow to read is waited on in reasonable time. With one, MAME counts the firings and stops only at a picture this wait has not yet rejected.

A wait that gives up never leaves the machine running: the last run is stopped first. If the screen is already there the reply comes at once, except under `on_breakpoint` or `on_watch`, where the first firing is awaited even so.
why_more:
- `waited_on` repeats what was waited on: its `kind`, its `ref`, and the `condition` if any.
- `fired_line` is the screen line being drawn at the firing that counted, or unavailable when no firing met the `condition`.
- `palette` and `entries` come with a black palette: the value asked for, and how many palette entries were read.
- Under `on_breakpoint` or `on_watch`, these fields replace `polls` and `sampled_every`.

breakpoint_at.what: Set a breakpoint at a symbol or an address, to stop there or to count how often the code runs.
breakpoint_at.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped with a credit in and the example session's symbol file loaded, which names the routine `take_credit`.
breakpoint_at.ask: Stop the game where it takes a credit to start a game.

then.lead: Then press START, held for four frames:

breakpoint_at.reads: The breakpoint is armed at `0xd676`. Pressing START ends in `OTHER_STOP`, a stop the call did not ask for: `cause` names the breakpoint on `take_credit`.

arguments.ref: Where to break: a symbol or a `0x` address in the code. Never an expression.
arguments.by: How `ref` is read: `symbol` or `address` forces one. Left at `auto`, a `0x` ref is an address and anything else a symbol.
arguments.role: `stop` halts the machine there. `control` never halts: it counts each time the code runs, for `run_to` to read.
arguments.condition: For a `stop` only: a debugger expression that must hold for the stop, such as `d0==1`. Bare numbers are hex.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose code holds the breakpoint. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.state: `armed` once the debugger lists it enabled, `unresolved` while `ref` names no symbol of this build. The top of the page lists the rest.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for the breakpoint, once armed.
returns.addr: The address `ref` resolves to, once it does.
returns.stored: `true` when the server saved the breakpoint. It is set again at the next `start`.
returns.already_stored: `true` when the same breakpoint was saved already, so the call changed nothing.
returns.temp: For a `control`, the debugger variable that counts its hits, `temp0` to `temp9`.

refuses: A `ref` with a segment (`seg:off`): an address here is one `0x` number (`bad_argument`).
A `condition` the debugger cannot evaluate, or one that holds `,`, `;`, braces or an assignment (`bad_argument`).
A `condition` too long for one console command: `command_chars` and `limit_chars` say by how much (`bad_argument`).
A `condition` on a `control`, which counts every hit (`bad_argument`).
A cpu the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
An address another saved breakpoint already holds, or the same `ref` under the other role or another condition (`ambiguous_ref`).
An eleventh `control`: the debugger has ten variables to count with (`bad_argument`).
A breakpoint the debugger took and does not list back: nothing is armed, and it stays saved as `gone` (`readback_refused`).
why: A `control` is for an address you know runs. `run_to` counts it beside its target, so a target never reached can be told from code that never ran. MAME counts the hits inside the debugger without halting, so a control costs a run nothing.

A `condition` makes one run out of many: "stop at the vblank handler once this variable reads X" is a single `resume`. It is saved as typed, like `ref`, so after a rebuild a symbol in it is compared where it now lives.

The condition is evaluated once before the breakpoint is set, because the debugger accepts a condition it cannot evaluate and that breakpoint never fires. A name that is both a symbol and a register of that cpu is refused as ambiguous.
why_more:
- A breakpoint set while the machine runs fires at once. `while_running` says the machine was running when the call came.
- `run_to` saves its own `control` as one, so every later run counts it too.
- A stop no instruction caused (the end of a frame, a time, a step) lands on an instruction whose breakpoints some MAME builds skip. A `control` there misses that hit.
- A run by frames lands on one such instruction every frame, often the first of the vblank handler. Put a control somewhere else.
- `condition` is the condition as the debugger reads it, your symbols replaced by addresses. `condition_typed` is what you typed, when the two differ.
- The condition is evaluated on the breakpoint's own cpu: the server makes it the visible one for that and puts the visible one back, which runs nothing.
- If the visible cpu cannot be put back, the call is refused before anything is saved and `visible_cpu` names the cpu left visible (`unexpected_answer`).
- At `start`, a saved condition the debugger cannot evaluate is reported `unresolved` when it names a symbol this build lacks and `unarmable` otherwise. It stays saved either way.
- `cpu` is the cpu the breakpoint is on. `note` warns when the debugger is set to ignore that cpu: the breakpoint has no effect until `debug("observe <cpu>")`.
- Each row is armed naming its cpu, `bp <addr>:<cpu>`, which never changes the visible cpu, at `start`'s re-arm too. A saved row with no cpu is the first cpu's.
- A row the debugger already lists there on that cpu, under the same condition and held by no other declaration, is taken over, not doubled, here and at `start`'s re-arm.
- A row `bplist` shows without the condition sent is not armed: the call is refused, and `start`'s re-arm lists it `unarmable`. Watches follow the same rule.

regpoint_add.what: Stop the machine when a condition on the registers comes true, wherever the program is, to find who puts a value in a register.
regpoint_add.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at `take_credit`, the routine that takes a credit when START is pressed.
regpoint_add.ask: Stop as soon as register A holds 0x99.

then.lead: Then run for one frame at most:

regpoint_add.reads: A bare number in a condition is hex, so `a==99` compares with 0x99. The run ends in `OTHER_STOP`, a stop it did not ask for, with `pc` at `0xd67b`.

arguments.condition: The condition, in the debugger's own expression grammar, where a bare number is hex: `d1==0x7fff`. It compares and never assigns.
arguments.cpu: Only the cpu the debugger is showing, which is also what leaving it empty means. Another cpu is refused, naming `cpu_focus`.

returns.state: `armed` once the debugger lists it enabled. The top of the page lists the rest.
returns.ref: The condition as typed. `declaration_clear` takes it.
returns.condition: The condition as the debugger read it, your symbols replaced by their addresses.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for the registerpoint.
returns.index: The debugger's row number for it.
returns.already_stored: `true` when the same registerpoint was saved already, so the call changed nothing.

refuses: A condition the debugger cannot evaluate, or one that assigns or holds `,`, `;` or braces (`bad_argument`).
A condition too long for one console command: `command_chars` and `limit_chars` say by how much (`bad_argument`).
A `cpu` that is not the one the debugger is showing: `cpu_focus` first (`needs_call`).
A condition that reads the same as another saved registerpoint's once symbols are replaced (`ambiguous_ref`).
A MAME whose debugger has no `rpset` command (`no_channel`).
A registerpoint the debugger took and does not list back: it stays saved as `gone` (`readback_refused`).
why: A registerpoint has no address, so it is never `stale` or `aliased` and has no `role`. `run_to` and `run_for` answer `OTHER_STOP`, a stop the run did not ask for, because a registerpoint is never a run's target.

It is evaluated after every instruction, so while the condition stays true it fires again one instruction later. The stop's `cause` reads `registerpoint '<ref>'`, and `regpoint_hit` holds the details.
The condition is evaluated once before it is saved, because the debugger accepts a registerpoint it cannot evaluate and that one never fires.
why_more:
- It belongs to the cpu the debugger is showing, because MAME's `rpset` names no cpu. At `start` it is set again only if its cpu is then the visible one.
- At `start` each saved condition is evaluated again: `unresolved` when the debugger answers `unknown symbol`, otherwise `unarmable`. One that fails does not stop the others.
- Saving the same condition again takes over the debugger's existing row only on the visible cpu. The same text under another cpu compares other registers and is left `foreign`.
- It works while the machine runs and does not mark the session `altered`, which means written to.
- `rpset {<condition>}` typed through `debug` does not mark it either, but an action after the condition counts as a write.
- `by` is always `expr`, and `while_running` says the machine was running when the call came.

watch_add.what: Keep a variable in view at every stop, stop the machine when it is written, or count every write to it, by name.
watch_add.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped in its coin routine right after a coin was counted, with the example session's symbol file loaded.
watch_add.ask: Stop the game when the BCD copy of the credits is written, and tell me which instruction did it.

then.lead: Then run for one frame at most:

watch_add.reads: `OTHER_STOP` is a stop the run did not ask for: here, the watch. The writer is at `0xb58c`; `pc` is the instruction after it, since the write has landed.

head: mode
what it does
stops?
rows: Reads the value at every stop.
Stops when the bytes are written.
Evaluates one debugger expression at every stop.
Counts every write and which instruction made it.
Logs a row per access, with the screen line being drawn and the time.

arguments.ref: What to watch: a symbol, a `0x` address, or an address reached through a pointer (`[base]+0x28`, `base->field`). For `expr`, the expression itself.
arguments.length: Total bytes; not needed when `fmt` has a size or the symbol has a type. At most 128 for `show` and `capture`, 1024 for the others.
arguments.fmt: How the bytes read: a scalar (`u8` to `f64`), an array (`u16[8]`), a string (`char[16]`) or a struct (`{x:i16,y:i16}`).
arguments.by: How `ref` is read: `symbol`, `address` or `pointer` forces one; `auto` lets the server choose.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory is watched. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.condition: For `change` only: a debugger expression that must hold for the stop, where `wpdata` is the value written: `wpdata==0x7f`.
arguments.trigger: For `capture` only: the address whose every write takes a row holding the block at `ref`.
arguments.space: `io` watches a port instead of memory: `count` or `capture` only, and for this session only.
arguments.trigger_type: `w` takes writes. On a `capture`, `r` takes reads of `ref` itself, with no `trigger`, `length` or `fmt`; on a `count`, `r` or `rw` counts reads too.

returns.state: `armed` for a `change` watch set in the debugger, `evaluated` for `show` and `expr`, `pending` for `count` and `capture`. The top of the page lists the rest.
returns.reading: What this call read at `ref`, on a stopped machine: `value` and `raw_hex`, or `available: false` with the reason, never a zero.
returns.entry: The debugger's own row for the watch, once armed.
returns.stored: The server saved the watch, and sets it again at `start`. `false` for a port watch.
returns.installed: `false` for a `count` or `capture` just sent: MAME installs it when its console next reads a line, and `pending` stays `true` until then.
returns.values_from: `bus` when the address does not read back what is written to it, as a write-only register: the values are then the writes logged, never a memory read.

refuses: A `change` watch where nothing handles the write, such as the ROM copy of a variable (`bad_argument`).
A `count` range that covers part of a bus word, such as a word at an odd address on a 16-bit bus (`bad_argument`).
One `ref` under two modes, sizes, formats, conditions or triggers: clear the first (`ambiguous_ref`).
A `change` watch that shares a byte with another armed one on the same cpu, or a `count` on a range already counted (`ambiguous_ref`).
A pointer base or a `trigger` that names no symbol, or a cpu the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
A watch through a pointer while the machine runs (`not_stopped`).
A `count` or `capture` through a pointer, or a `capture` block with a handler inside it (`bad_argument`).
A `length` over the mode's maximum, or none where neither `fmt` nor the symbol gives a size (`bad_argument`).
`condition` on any mode but `change`, `trigger` on any mode but `capture`, and a write capture without one (`bad_argument`).
On a port: `show`, `change`, `expr` or a count of reads, or a cpu with no io space (`bad_argument`).
A `change` watch the debugger took and does not list back: nothing is saved (`readback_refused`).
why: A `change` watch answers "who wrote this byte". The write has landed when the machine stops, so the stop's `pc` is the instruction after the writer. The stop's `watch_hit` names the writer and each write since the previous stop.
`count` and `capture` exist for what a stop cannot give: every value a variable takes over a stretch, and who wrote each, while the program keeps running.

`state` says where the watch stands and `reading` what this call read, since a `change` watch is armed and read at the same stop. One `ref` carries one watch per cpu: another mode, size, format, condition or trigger under it is refused until cleared.
why_more: On every watch:

- An address matches in any spelling; a symbol and its address are two refs.
- A region is `memdump`'s job, which is why lengths are limited.
- With `fmt` left at `auto`, a typed symbol reads as its type, else as the widest unsigned scalar that divides `length`.
- Arming writes nothing to the machine, so the session is not `altered`.
- A watch set while the machine runs is armed at once and fires. Only a ref through a pointer needs a stop.
- `reading` holds `available`, then `value` and `raw_hex` (`value` and `hex` for an `expr`), or `why` when nothing could be read.
On `show` and `expr`:

- A watch on another cpu is read only on a MAME whose gdbstub reads every cpu. Otherwise its `reading` is `available: false`, and a watch through a pointer there is refused.
- Every `expr` is read in one `print` at each stop, so one more costs a stop nothing.
- An `expr` has no cpu, and takes no `,`, `;`, assignment, `length` or `fmt`.
On `change`:

- The writer comes from the debugger's own log line for the stop. A 68000 writes a long as two words, so one write lists as two.
- The debugger accepts a watchpoint on the ROM copy of a variable whose live copy is in RAM, and it never fires. So the memory map is asked first.
- Two watchpoints on one byte would make "who wrote it" ambiguous, so an overlap is refused. A `count` or a `capture` never stops, so only an identical one is refused.
- The debugger's list is read back after every arm, and a watch is saved only once it is armed.
- For a write-only register a stop's reading is `bus` with `last_wrote`, the last value written.
- `write_maps_to` and `read_maps_to` say what the memory map has at the address for each direction.
- The writer's `pc` is a `0x` address, so it goes straight into `disassemble` or `breakpoint_at` as a `ref`. MAME names it only for a write by the watch's own cpu.
On a `condition`:

- It answers "who writes bits 0-1 of this byte" without a stop at every write of the register.
- `wpdata` is the value as it reached the bus, shifted down to the bytes written.
