- It takes `breakpoint_at`'s grammar on the watch's cpu and is evaluated once before arming: MAME sets a watchpoint whose condition it cannot evaluate, and that one never fires.
- A watch through a pointer that is still null has its condition checked right away: the stop that finds the pointer set has no call left to refuse it.
- A row the debugger lists without the condition sent is `readback_refused`. A row already at that range under another condition is `ambiguous_ref`.
On `count`:

- It sees the writes of its own cpu only, never those a DMA or a blitter makes on its own bus.
- It counts writes to its own range only. To count one register's values by the value of another, use a `capture`: two counts cannot be joined afterwards.
- A write lands in one bus word, so a word covered in part would give fragments with no `value`. That is why such a range is refused.
- It sees every write the cpu makes, handled or not, so it arms where nothing handles the write: `write_maps_to` is then `unmapped`, with a `note`.
- `tally_id` names it: its range, plus the cpu when that is not the first one.
- A count that never started must not read as zero. An install the console echoed and never ran is sent once more (`install_resent`); lost twice, the state is `install_lost`.
- `lines_ahead` is how many console lines wait before the install, and `call` the line that marks it done.
- Declaring the range again installs over the old count and keeps its counts. After a clear that ran, it counts from zero.
- A count or capture whose periodic write keeps failing leaves its last finished dump on disk. Its reading is `superseded`, its `why` the error `error.log` logs as `MCP_DUMP_FAILED`.
On `capture`:

- The row is taken before the write lands. When `trigger` lies inside the block, the block holds the value from before the write.
- The block must be plain memory. Reading through a handler would run it at every trigger, and reading around it gives zeros that look like data.
- `source` says where the block is read: `kind`, then `addr` in the cpu's memory, or the `tag` and `offset` of a memory share or region.
- `time_s` is the accessing cpu's own clock at full precision, so two accesses one cycle apart never share it.
- Captures on two cpus share one clock: order their rows by `time_s`, not by position. `line` is the screen line being drawn.
- A capture of reads keeps the access and no block. It sees no instruction fetch and no ROM read, so on code or ROM it keeps no row.
- It runs at every read, so on an address the program polls it costs a Lua call per poll.
- A read capture's `ref` is its trigger, so a write capture of the same address under that ref is refused.
- `gfx_blits`, `gfx_blit_source`, `gfx_draft` and a region write read write captures only.
- `trigger_addr` is where `trigger` resolves, and `trigger_maps_to` what the memory map has there.
On a port (`space="io"`):

- A board that drives its palette or sound through `out` writes nothing to program memory, so only a port watch sees it.
- It lasts the session only. The saved breakpoints file knows no ports, and would set it again as the memory address of the same number.
- It is cleared with its `ref` and `space="io"`. Its `tally_id` carries the space (`6_2@io`): port 6 and address 6 are two watches.
- `cpus_with_io` lists the cpus that have ports, when the one named has none.
Through a pointer:

- It reaches a field a C program keeps in a heap struct behind a global pointer.
- The pointer is read at the width its type gives (`ptr16{...}`, `ptr32{...}`), else at the stack pointer's width.
- On a board whose symbol file sets `bases`, a pointer read through a symbol of a relocated class is an offset in that class's segment.
- A type can name the class (`ptr16@CODE`), which a routine's address kept in DATA needs.
- It is followed again at every stop. A `change` watch moves with it (`moved`), and a null pointer is `null_pointer`, never a watch at address zero.
- `pointer` holds where the pointer was read (`at`, `length`), its `value`, the `offset` and `field` added, and `relocated` (`class`, `base`, `class_from`).

declaration_list.what: List the saved breakpoints, registerpoints and watches, each with its state checked against the debugger's own list.
declaration_list.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, after the breakpoint, the registerpoint and the watch of the other entries were set, and a `run_to` left its control.
declaration_list.ask: Which breakpoints and watches are set right now?
declaration_list.reads: Two breakpoints, one registerpoint and one watch are saved, and the debugger lists each as armed. No cpu was named, so the rows are every cpu's.

arguments.cpu: Narrows the rows to one cpu. Left empty, every cpu's.

returns.breakpoints: The saved breakpoints. Each row has `ref`, `role`, `addr`, `state` and, once armed, the debugger's `entry`.
returns.regpoints: The saved registerpoints, each with its `condition`, `state`, `entry` and the debugger's `index`.
returns.watches: The saved watches, each with `mode`, `length`, `fmt` and `state`. A `count` or a `capture` adds its tables.
returns.foreign: Debugger rows the server did not set, by kind, as the debugger lists them. They are listed and never deleted.
returns.cpu: The cpu the rows were narrowed to, or `available: false` when none was named.

refuses: A cpu the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
why: It answers while the machine runs, and each state is the machine's own answer: every call reads the debugger's breakpoint, watchpoint and registerpoint lists back.

`inherited` is `true` on a row an earlier session saved, since no reply names this session to compare with. `age_s` counts the seconds since `created_at`; a date ahead of this computer's clock gives a negative age, never a zero that would read as "now".
why_more: What a row carries:

- Every row: `ref`, `by` (how the ref is read), `cpu`, `created_at`, `origin` (the session that saved it), `inherited`, `age_s`, `state`, and `why` where the state needs a reason.
- A breakpoint adds `role`, `addr`, `entry`, its `condition` (with `condition_typed` when the debugger reads it differently) and a control's `hits_since_armed`.
- A registerpoint adds `condition`, `entry` and `index`.
- A watch adds `mode`, `length`, `fmt`, `addr`, `reading` on a stopped machine, `pointer` for a ref through one, and a `change` watch's `entry` and `values_from`.
- A `count` or a `capture` adds `tally_id`, `installed`, `pending`, `install_resent`, `call`, `total`, `frame_as_of` and `superseded`.
- A `count` adds `values` (each `at`, `raw_hex`, `count`, and `value` or `partial`), `values_total` and `overflow_values`.
- It also adds `writers` (each `pc`, `count`, `symbol`), `writers_total`, `overflow_pcs`, and `reads` when it counts them.
- A `capture` adds `trigger`, `trigger_addr`, `trigger_type`, `source`, `rows_path`, `rows_kept`, `rows_max`, `overflow_rows` and `first_rows`.
- Each of `first_rows` has `n`, `frame`, `line`, `time_s`, `pc`, `symbol`, `data`, `mask`, and a write capture's `raw_hex` and `block`.
- A port watch adds `space` and `stored: false`.
- A reset or a state load under a count adds `across` (`event`, `frame_from`): its totals then span two runs.
- A callback that raised adds `callback_errors` (`count`, `first`). While the machine runs the reply adds `last_stop`.
The states of a `count` or a `capture`, beside those at the top of the page:

| `state` | what it means |
|---|---|
| `tallied`, `captured` | Installed, and its tables were read. |
| `no_dump_yet` | Nothing is on disk yet: MAME writes the tables at a stop. |
| `not_installed` | This session holds none for it: `start` did not send it, or it was cleared. |
| `install_failed` | MAME ran the install and it failed. `why` has the error. |
| `install_lost` | MAME's console never ran the install, twice. It recorded nothing: clear it and declare it again. |
What the tables say:

- `values` and `writers` add up from the install on. A write that found its table full is counted in `overflow_values` or `overflow_pcs` and not named.
- A capture's `total` counts every access to its trigger: `rows_kept` of them have a row, and `overflow_rows` came after the limit `rows_max`.
- The listing shows a capture's first rows only, since each holds a whole block. `rows_path` is the file with every row.
- `superseded` is `true` when the tables on disk are older than the frame the machine stands at. `frame_as_of` is the frame they were written at.
- A stop's reply adds `since_last_stop`, and `reset` when the total fell, and never the rows or tables. A listing between two stops uses up nothing.

declaration_clear.what: Remove saved breakpoints, registerpoints or watches: one by its `ref`, or every one of a kind.
declaration_clear.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, with two breakpoints saved: one on `take_credit`, and the control an earlier `run_to` left on `wait_frame`.
declaration_clear.reads: Both saved breakpoints are gone, and `disarmed` shows the two debugger rows removed. The first was the control: its condition counts in `temp0` and never comes true.

arguments.ref: The one to clear, as the reply that saved it gave its `ref`. Left empty with `all=True`.
arguments.cpu: Clear on this cpu only. Left empty, on every cpu.
arguments.all: `true` clears every one of `kind`, and takes no `ref`.
arguments.space: `io` when `ref` is a port watch. Only `watch` takes it.

returns.declarations_cleared: How many were removed from the saved breakpoints file.
returns.disarmed: The debugger rows removed, as the debugger listed them, checked by reading its list back.
returns.tallies_removed: The `count` and `capture` watches whose removal was sent to MAME, each with `tally_id`, `removal`, `lines_ahead` and `call`.
returns.while_running: `true` when the machine was running as the call arrived. The clear works either way.

refuses: An empty `ref` without `all`, or both together (`bad_argument`).
A `ref` that matches nothing: the message names the refs saved (`unknown_ref`).
`space` on a kind other than `watch`, or together with `all` (`bad_argument`).
why: It removes only what this server set: a `foreign` row, one typed through `debug`, is never deleted.
A `ref` is read once, so a clear reaches only its own kind, and a name is never taken for the address its letters spell. An address matches in any spelling; a symbol must be the one saved.

With no `cpu` it reaches that `ref` on every cpu. In a file several sessions use, `all=True` also clears rows another session saved, which read `inherited: true`: clear by `ref` when they are not yours.
why_more:
- Removing a `count` or a `capture` is sent to MAME's console and applied when it next reads a line.
- It is never sent twice: the id is the range, and a second send could remove a watch declared since.
- A removal MAME did not carry out shows on every reply under `session.tallies_not_removed`.
- If the debugger still lists a row after its removal, `note` says so and names the `debug` command that removes it.
- `all=True` on `watch` removes the port watches too.
- A registerpoint's condition or an `expr` watch matches as typed but for its numbers, read as the console reads them: `7fff`, `0x7fff`, `$7fff` and `#32767` are one.
- There a run of letters such as `ab` stays a name and keeps its case. A saved address written in bare hex is that address.
- With a `state_dir`, `all=True` reaches only the rows saved in that folder. Without one, it reaches every session's rows of the same system and symbol file.
- Declaring the range again installs over a count not removed, keeping its totals, and a clear then removes it. Its `tallies_not_removed` row stays: this session counted past a removal.

read_memory.what: Read a few bytes of memory at an address, as hex text.
read_memory.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset, right after `start`.
read_memory.ask: Read the two bytes of the IRQ vector, at 0xfff8.
read_memory.reads: The two bytes at `0xfff8` are `fd80`. They are the cpu's IRQ vector, so the interrupt routine starts at `0xfd80`.

arguments.ref: The address to read: a symbol or a `0x` address.
arguments.length: How many bytes: 1 to 1024. Left out, 16.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose program memory is read. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.hex: The bytes, two hex characters each, lowest address first.

refuses: A range that runs past the cpu's program memory (`bad_argument`).
why: The reply is hex text in the conversation, so it is kept short: a screen's worth of video memory would bury everything else. For more, `memdump` writes the bytes to a file.
Memory the board can only write to reads back as zeros, with no error, because its values sit behind the write handler. `symbols_find` marks such an address `latch`, and `read_block` reads it.

read_block.what: Read bytes MAME keeps under a tag and no cpu can read back: write-only memory, or a ROM outside every cpu's address space.
read_block.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped once the game has drawn its sprites; the example session reads at frame 545.
read_block.ask: Read four bytes of the sprite memory, from its byte 12 on.
read_block.reads: `spriteram` is a share, a block MAME keeps by name, 2048 bytes long. The four bytes from offset 12 are `5b009394`, one sprite's entry.

arguments.tag: The block's name in MAME, `blitram` or `:blitram`. Give this or `ref`, never both.
arguments.ref: An address inside the block, instead of its tag: a symbol or a `0x` address whose address-map entry names the block.
arguments.offset: Where to start inside the block, with `tag`: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, its first byte.
arguments.length: How many bytes: 1 to 1024. Left out, 16.
arguments.seconds: How long MAME's Lua console may take to answer. Left out, 5 seconds.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose address map `ref` is looked up in. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.hex: The bytes, two hex characters each.
returns.kind: `share` or `region`, MAME's two words for such a block.
returns.tag: The block's tag as MAME spells it in full.
returns.offset: Where the read began inside the block. With `ref`, the address's distance into it.
returns.start: With `ref`: the first address of the map entry that names the block. `addr` and `addr_cpu` say what `ref` resolved to, and on which cpu.

refuses: Both `tag` and `ref`, or neither; `offset` with `ref`; `cpu` with `tag`; a `tag` holding whitespace (`bad_argument`).
A read that runs past the block's end (`bad_argument`).
A tag the machine does not have; the refusal's `tags` lists the ones it has (`unknown_ref`).
A `ref` no address-map entry covers, or whose entry names no block; `map_entry` then gives that entry's `start` and `end` (`unknown_ref`).
why: MAME keeps by tag two kinds of block that `read_memory` cannot reach. Memory that a handler only writes to, which MAME calls a share, answers zeros there. A ROM outside every cpu's address space, a region such as `gfx1`, is not there at all.
The bytes are the block after the instruction the read runs. To see the block as a write found it, stop one instruction earlier.
Past a block's end MAME answers zeros without complaint, which is why a read that runs past it is refused.

registers.what: Read the cpu's registers, now or as they were at the last stop.
registers.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped by a watch right after the game wrote its third credit.
registers.ask: Show me the cpu's registers at this stop.
registers.reads: Gridlee's cpu has ten registers. The whole reply, folded below, lists each under `regs`, and its width in bits under `register_bits`.

arguments.from_last_stop: `true` returns the registers the last stop recorded, and answers while the program runs. Left out, the registers are read now.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose registers are read. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.regs: Each register by name, as a hex string of its own width.
returns.register_bits: Each register's own width in bits.
returns.superseded: `true` with `from_last_stop`: the values are the last stop's, which `last_stop` identifies, not the current ones.
returns.cpu: The cpu the registers belong to.

refuses: `from_last_stop` together with `cpu` (`bad_argument`).
`from_last_stop` before the session's first stop (`no_stop`).
A cpu whose registers MAME's gdbstub does not describe (`no_channel`).
why: Each value is printed at its register's own width, and `register_bits` states it, because a fixed eight digits would make a 16-bit register look 32-bit. A V30's 16-bit register is named `EAX` and says 16.

The names are the ones MAME's gdbstub gives the cpu. A 68000 has `D0` to `D7`, `A0` to `A5`, `FP`, `SP`, `PS` and `PC`; an x86 or a V30 has `EAX` to `GS` with `EIP`. `set_register` also takes the 68000 aliases `A6`, `A7`, `SR` and `USP`, which are not listed here.
why_more: The byte order is MAME's: the endianness of the cpu's program space, as `start` read it. It is not established when that read failed, or when it disagrees with the order measured for that architecture, and the cpu is then `no_channel`.
At a stop, the `regs` of such a cpu say `available: false` with a `why`, never another cpu's registers under its name.

disassemble.what: Disassemble the code at an address, one instruction a line, each marked as a call, a branch, a return or none of those.
disassemble.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset with the example session's symbol file loaded, which names `count_coin`.
disassemble.ask: Show me the first instructions of the routine that counts a coin.
disassemble.reads: Five instructions from `0xb583`: the routine adds one to `$042B`, then to the decimal copy at `$042C`. Gridlee's cpu is a 6809, one with no mnemonic table, so no line is classified and `note` says why.

arguments.ref: Where to start: a symbol or a `0x` address.
arguments.length: How many bytes to decode, 1 to 1024; left out, 16. The last instruction is completed even when it runs past them.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose code is read. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.lines: One instruction a line, as MAME's `dasm` prints it: address, bytes, text. A line with a comment ends ` // <text>`.
returns.flow_source: What classified the lines: `mnemonic_table:<cpu type>`, or `none` with a `note` saying why no line was classified.
returns.resolved: Only when `start` was given `bases`: each direct memory operand as the address the board uses. Rows carry `line`, `operand`, `offset`, `class`, `linear`, `symbol` and `delta`.

refuses: A listing MAME's console did not write, or wrote empty (`unexpected_answer`).
why: `flow` is read off each mnemonic with a table per cpu type, because MAME's console does not say which instructions call or return.

On a segmented board MAME prints an operand as an offset inside its segment. `resolved` gives the address the board uses as `linear`, which `read_memory` and `watch_add` take, once per symbol class that has a base. An operand relative to a register is not resolved: its address is the register's value at run time.
A word MAME cannot decode is marked by MAME itself: `dc.w ...; ILLEGAL`.

find.what: Find every address in a range of memory that holds a given sequence of bytes.
find.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset, right after `start`.
find.ask: Find where the ROM holds the bytes 7c 04 2b, the instruction that adds one to the credits.
find.reads: One address holds those bytes, `0xb583`. `span` says which bytes were searched: 24576 from `0xa000`, the whole ROM.

arguments.data_hex: The bytes to look for, as hex: 1 to 126 whole bytes.
arguments.ref: Where the range begins: a symbol or a `0x` address. Give it with `length`, or give `symbol_class` instead.
arguments.length: How many bytes to search from `ref`.
arguments.symbol_class: A class of the symbol file, `DATA` or `CODE` say, searched from its first symbol to its last. It replaces `ref` and `length`.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose program memory is searched. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.hits: The addresses where the bytes begin, at most 400; past that, the highest are kept.
returns.hits_total: How many addresses hold the bytes, listed or not.
returns.truncated: `true` when there are more hits than `hits` lists.
returns.span: The bytes that were searched, as `from`, `length` and `source`, so zero hits says where there are none.

refuses: Both `symbol_class` and a `ref` with `length`, or neither (`bad_argument`).
A class the symbol file does not have (`unknown_ref`).
More than 126 bytes in `data_hex`, or hex that is not whole bytes (`bad_argument`).
A range that runs past the cpu's program memory (`bad_argument`).
A console answer that is neither hits nor `Not found` (`unexpected_answer`).
why: A hit is where the bytes begin, so a match that starts inside the range and runs past its end counts.
A linker map gives no sizes, so a class is searched only up to the start of its last symbol; `span` carries a `note` saying so.
There is no search of the whole address space, because the symbol file does not say where it ends. MAME's console takes each byte as a parameter of its own, which limits them to 126.

history.what: List the last instructions a cpu ran before the stop, oldest first.
history.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped by a watch right after the game wrote its third credit.
history.ask: What were the last eight instructions the cpu ran before this stop?
history.reads: Oldest first: the call at `B57C` into the coin routine, then the routine's own instructions from `B583` on. All eight asked for came back.

arguments.limit: How many instructions back: 1 to 256, the most MAME keeps for a cpu. Left out, 32.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose instructions are listed. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.lines: One instruction a line, `<address>: <instruction>`, oldest first. Fewer than asked means the cpu has run no more.
returns.cpu: The cpu the instructions belong to.

refuses: A cpu MAME has no disassembler for (`no_channel`).
A console answer that is not a list of instructions (`unexpected_answer`).
why: A cpu that has run no instruction yet answers with no lines and a `note` saying so.

memdump.what: Write a range of memory to a file, for ranges too large to read into the conversation.
memdump.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at any moment: the range is ROM, which never changes.
memdump.ask: Save the first 4096 bytes of the ROM at 0xa000 to a file.
memdump.reads: The file holds 4096 bytes, as asked: `bytes` equals `length`. `path` is where it was written.

arguments.ref: Where the range begins: a symbol or a `0x` address.
arguments.dest: The file to create, required: an absolute or `~`-led path, in a folder that exists, not there yet. The path holds no space, comma, semicolon, quote or bracket.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose program memory is written out. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.path: The file as written; a `note` says so when its name is not the one `dest` gave.

refuses: A `dest` that is relative, already there, or in a folder that does not exist (`bad_argument`).
A range that runs past the cpu's program memory (`bad_argument`).
A file that is not `length` bytes, or whose first bytes differ from a direct read of the same memory (`readback_refused`).
A debugger connection that breaks during that direct read (`session_broken`).
why: MAME's own `save` command writes the file, so the bytes never pass through the debugger connection. The server then reads the first bytes of the range directly and compares them with the file, which is what shows the file holds the memory asked for.
A range that runs past the cpu's program memory would hang `save`, so it is refused before anything is written and leaves no file.

screen_map_find.what: Name the screen your program is showing, from its screen map: a file of the program's screens and the named areas of each.
screen_map_find.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped on the level card the game shows after START, just after the example of `screen_map_write` below added that screen.
screen_map_find.ask: Which screen of the map is the game showing?
screen_map_find.reads: The game shows `level_card`, one of the screens added this session (`layer` `session`). Its area `level` is the rectangle at 88, 152, with its centre at 124, 156.

returns.matched: `true` when a screen of the map is the one showing.
returns.screen: The name of the screen that matched.
returns.controls: The matched screen's named areas, each with `name`, `rect` and `centre`, in the program's own units.
returns.layer: Where the screen was found: `session` for a screen added in this session, `file` for one of the loaded map.
returns.screens_mapped: When nothing matched: how many screens the map holds. `screens_tried` says how many had the right kind and size.
returns.view_fits: `false` when the picture's size cannot be the map's, seen through the `scale` and `margin` it was loaded with.

refuses: No screen mapped yet: load a map or add a screen with `screen_map_write` (`needs_call`).
why: A screen matches when its kind and size are the ones showing and each of its regions has the fingerprint the map recorded. Screens added this session are tried first, then the loaded file's.
The screen is captured once for the whole map, and sizes are compared before any fingerprint: a capture is a round trip through MAME's Lua console.
A screen added with `cells` `index` is compared by palette index, not by colour. Capturing the indices costs MAME more, so it happens only when the map holds such a screen.

screen_map_write.what: Build the screen map, the file that names your program's screens and their areas: add the screen showing, load a file, or save one.
screen_map_write.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped on the level card the game shows after START is pressed with a credit in.
screen_map_write.ask: Add this screen to the map as level_card, known by its title, with the level number as an area named level.
screen_map_write.reads: The screen is recorded as `level_card`, 256 by 240 pixels, with one named area. Its one region has the fingerprint `5733a1938b03c102` (`signature`), which is what later identifies it.

head: method
what it does
rows: Records the screen showing now under a name, with the regions that identify it and its named areas. Needs the program stopped.
Reads a map file; nothing is written to disk. Works while the program runs.
Writes the loaded map and the screens added since as one file, which becomes the loaded map. Works while the program runs.

arguments.screen: For `add`: the name the screen is recorded under.
arguments.match: For `add`: 1 to 16 rectangles `[x, y, width, height]` that always look the same on this screen. They are what identifies it.
arguments.controls: For `add`: the screen's named areas, each `{"name", "rect"}`. Left out, none.
arguments.cells: For `add`: `index` compares palette indices, not the colours shown, so one map serves a program shown through two palettes. Left out, `rgb`.
arguments.anchor: For `add`: a symbol or an address the program reaches once the screen is fully drawn. `run_to(screen=)` runs to it.
arguments.path: For `load`: the map file, named `<application>-screen-map.json`, as an absolute or `~`-led path.
arguments.scale: For `load`: how many times larger this machine shows the program's picture, 1 to 8. Left out, 1.
arguments.margin: For `load`: `[x, y]`, the border in machine pixels on each side of the program's picture. Left out, none.
arguments.dest: For `save`: the file to write, named `<application>-screen-map.json`, as an absolute or `~`-led path.
arguments.overwrite: For `save`: `true` replaces a file already at `dest`. Left out, an existing file is refused.

returns.match: `add`: each region as recorded, with its `crop` and its `signature`, the fingerprint taken from the screen.
returns.replaced: `add`: `true` when a screen of that name was already added this session. `shadows_file` is `true` when the loaded file has one too.
returns.kept: `add`: reads `N saved for promote` once the map is a candidate that `promote` can write into your repository's `.scry/` folder.
returns.screens: `load` and `save`: how many screens the map holds; `controls` counts their named areas.
returns.mode: `load` and `save`: `verified` when a screen is checked each time it is reached, `consolidated` when it is trusted without a check.
returns.promoted: `save`: the names of the screens added this session that the file now holds.

refuses: An argument the method does not take.
A name, rectangle, area or file that is not well formed, or a rectangle outside the screen (`bad_argument`).
An `add` without `anchor` when the loaded map is `consolidated`, or a `save` of one holding a screen with none (`bad_argument`).
`cells` `index` on a screen that has no palette (`no_channel`).
A `save` with nothing mapped (`needs_call`).
why: A screen is recognised by a few regions that never change, not by the whole picture: a cursor or a moving ball would change a fingerprint of the whole screen.

The map has two layers. Screens you `add` live in the session and win over a loaded file's screen of the same name; `save` writes both as one file. A new `start` empties the session layer and keeps the file.

A map's `mode` says who keeps it true. In a `verified` map, `run_to(screen=)` checks the screen's regions on reaching it and refuses a map that no longer matches (`stale_map`). In a `consolidated` map the screen is trusted at its `anchor`, which lets one map serve two versions of a program whose pixels differ.
why_more: The mode is the file's own: `save` keeps the loaded map's, and writes `verified` when none was loaded. `screen_map_find` checks the regions in either mode.

Rectangles are in the program's pixels. With `scale` and `margin`, this machine's picture is the program's size times the scale, plus the margin on each side. A capture is sampled back to the program's size before it is compared.
A map file is kept in the program's repository, as `.scry/maps/<application>-screen-map.json`, and looks like this.

```json
{"format": "scry-screen-map/1", "application": "circus", "mode": "verified",
 "screens": [{"name": "attract", "kind": "pixel", "size": [248, 256],
              "match": [{"crop": [0, 0, 248, 8], "signature": "<16 hex>"}],
              "controls": [{"name": "high_score", "rect": [40, 112, 184, 8]}]}]}
```

On an arcade board a named area is somewhere to read, never something to click: its inputs go in by port and field. A file may also say where the program keeps a mouse pointer; this server keeps that entry, writes it back on `save` and does nothing else with it.

In the replay test `perform_export` writes, `load` and `add` are replayed as steps and `screen_map_find` becomes a check of what it matched. A `save` is left out, since a replay would find its file there.

palette.what: Read the colours the palette holds now, as a list and as a picture of colour swatches.

arguments.palette: The palette device to read, by its MAME tag. Left empty, the machine's only one.
arguments.first: The first entry to read: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, 0.
arguments.count: How many entries to read, at most 256. Left at 0, to the end; read a larger palette in pages, with `first`.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, 1 to 8. Left at 0, the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 5.

returns.colors: Each entry read, as `#rrggbb`, in order from `first`.
returns.entries: How many entries the palette has.
returns.truncated: `true` when a read to the end stopped at 256 entries with more left.
returns.alpha: Each entry's alpha, listed only when some entry is not fully opaque.
returns.indirect_entries: How many entries MAME's second, indirect colour table holds for this device.
returns.image: The PNG: its `path`, `bytes`, `sha256`, `width`, `height` and `scale`, whether it is `indexed`, and `inline` or the reason in `not_inlined`.

refuses: A `palette` tag the machine does not have; the refusal lists its `palettes` (`unknown_ref`).
An empty `palette` on a machine with several palette devices (`ambiguous_ref`) or with none (`no_channel`).
A `first` and `count` that reach past the last entry (`bad_argument`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: The colours come from MAME's own palette device, the entries the screen is drawn with. On many boards nothing else can be read: a RAMDAC is write-only, and some drivers keep their colours in an array of their own.

The read costs one instruction of the program: MAME's console runs a line only when the machine moves, so the call steps once and reads after it. Nothing is altered. The reply is also a stop, and `pc_before` says where the program stood.
In the picture each row holds 16 entries, with the index of its first entry written at its left in hexadecimal, so no entry has to be counted across.
why_more: `shadows` and `highlights` say whether the device has those two of MAME's tables on. The fields about MAME's console (`evaluated_by`, `lines_ahead`, `reader_steps`, `resent`, `thread_errors`, `console_reruns`, `call`) are explained on the [Lua](lua.md) page.
palette.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped while its attract mode plays. Entry 838, in the range asked for, is the colour of a pixel of the player's sprite.
palette.ask: Show me the 32 palette entries from 832 on, and save the swatches as palette.png.
palette.reads: The summary's `pens` are palette entries: this palette has 2048, and the reply lists 32 of them, from 832 (`0x340`), as colours. The swatches went to a PNG enlarged 8 times.

screen_view.what: Read the screen at a stop: its picture, the pixels that hold chosen palette indices, the indices in use, or one pixel.

head: mode
what it answers
rows: The screen as a PNG. On a screen drawn through a palette, each pixel of the file is its palette index.
The picture with the palette indices in `pens` in magenta and every other pixel grey, and how many pixels hold them.
No picture: each palette index in use with how many pixels hold it, and the ranges nothing uses.
The palette index and the colour under `point`, with a small picture of the pixels round it.

arguments.pens: For `isolate`: the palette indices to show, 1 to 64 of them. A pen is the palette index a pixel holds.
arguments.point: For `pixel`: the pixel to read, `[x, y]` on the screen.
arguments.crop: The rectangle to read, `[x, y, width, height]`; not for `pixel`. Left out, the whole screen.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, 1 to 8; not for `histogram`. Left at 0, the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.attach: `false` writes the picture without attaching it to the reply. Left out, `true`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 5.

returns.image: The PNG: its `path`, `bytes`, `sha256`, `width`, `height` and `scale`, whether it is `indexed`, and `inline` or the reason in `not_inlined`. Not for `histogram`.
returns.screen_indexed: `true` when the screen is drawn through a palette. The PNG itself is indexed when that palette has at most 256 entries.
returns.pen: For `pixel`: the palette index under the point; `color` is the colour it shows.
returns.set_by: For `pixel`: the newest write `palette_log` recorded for that entry, or the reason there is none.
returns.histogram: For `histogram`: one `[pen, pixels]` pair for each palette index in use. `pens_used` counts them; `unused` lists the rest as ranges.
returns.pixels: For `isolate`: how many pixels hold the indices asked for. `bbox` is the rectangle that holds them all, as `[left, top, right, bottom]`.

refuses: An argument the mode does not take: `pens` outside `isolate`, `point` outside `pixel`, a picture argument with `histogram` (`bad_argument`).
A `crop` or a `point` off the screen (`bad_argument`).
`isolate`, `histogram` or `pixel` on a screen drawn in direct colour, which holds no palette index (`no_channel`).
A machine with no screen, a vector screen, or a palette with `shadows` or `highlights` on (`no_channel`).
A machine with several screens (`ambiguous_ref`).
A palette entry that did not read back as saved, or a screen that changed across the read (`readback_refused`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: A colour picture cannot say which palette index a pixel holds, and two entries can share a colour. MAME hands the screen back as colours, so one script saves every palette entry, sets entry `i` to the colour `i`, reads the screen and puts every entry back.

No instruction of the program runs inside that script, so the program never sees the changed palette, and the entries go back even when the read fails. The reply is refused, never drawn, when the picture cannot be trusted.
`isolate` draws the other pixels in greys with no black or white. Dimming would lose a dark entry in a dark screen, and one hue over greys stands out whatever the entry's colour.
why_more: The read costs one instruction of the program, as [`palette`](#palette) explains, and the reply is also a stop.

- Refused: an index past the palette's entries.
- Refused: a saved entry that is not the colour the screen showed, as under a contrast or gamma setting.
- Refused: an entry that did not read back. It counts as a write to the machine, and `pens_not_restored` lists it.
- Refused: a screen that changed across the read.

For `pixel`, `agrees` inside `set_by` says whether the colour that write left is the entry's colour now. When it is not, something other than a port write changed the entry: a driver copying entries itself, a Lua `set_pen_color`, a loaded state.
The reply then names `same_color_write`, the newest recorded write that left that colour; `rows_cut` says whether the log had lost rows.
For `pixel` the picture is a crop of 48 pixels round the point, in colour, with the point ringed and a `border` round the crop. `point_in_crop` is the point inside it.

A refusal names what it found: `screens` lists the screens of a machine with several, `screen_type` the kind of a screen that has no pixels to read. `frame_screen` is the screen's own frame number at the read.
The fields about MAME's console (`evaluated_by`, `lines_ahead`, `reader_steps`, `resent`, `thread_errors`, `console_reruns`, `call`) are explained on the [Lua](lua.md) page.
screen_view.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped while its attract mode plays. The point is a pixel of the player's sprite at that stop; any point of the 256x240 screen can be asked.
screen_view.ask: Which palette index does the pixel at 151, 172 hold, and what colour does it show?
screen_view.reads: The pixel holds `pen` 838, a palette index out of 2048 entries, which shows as `#449933`. The picture written is the 48-pixel square `crop` round the point, which sits at its centre.

screen_signature.what: Get a short hash of what the screen shows, so two screens can be told the same without comparing pictures.

arguments.crop: The rectangle to hash, `[x, y, width, height]`. Left out, the whole screen.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 5.

returns.signature: 16 hex characters. Two screens, or two crops of one size, show the same when their signatures are equal.

refuses: A `crop` that leaves the screen (`bad_argument`).
A machine with no screen, or a vector screen (`no_channel`).
A machine with several screens (`ambiguous_ref`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: The signature answers "is it the same screen" with two strings, never two pictures. A caller that waits for a screen, compares two moments or keeps a reference holds 16 characters, not a PNG.

It is made of the colour each pixel shows, never its palette index, so a palette change is a new signature and two screens that look the same have one. Only a screen map can be told to fingerprint palette indices ([`screen_map_write`](read.md#screen_map_write)).
`series_capture` writes the same signature for each frame it keeps, so a frame of a series and the screen now compare directly.
why_more: The format is `scry-sig/1`: BLAKE2b with an 8-byte digest, 16 lowercase hex characters. It covers the text `scry-sig/1|pixel|<w>x<h>|`, with the crop's size, and then the crop's pixels row by row as RGB.
The read costs one instruction of the program, as [`palette`](#palette) explains, and the reply is also a stop.

`kind` is `pixel`, `screen` is the screen's MAME tag and `frame_screen` its own frame number at the read. The fields about MAME's console (`evaluated_by`, `lines_ahead`, `reader_steps`, `resent`, `thread_errors`, `console_reruns`, `call`) are explained on the [Lua](lua.md) page.
screen_signature.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped five seconds after power-on, with its attract screen showing.
screen_signature.ask: Give me the signature of the screen as it is now, so I can tell later whether it changed.
screen_signature.reads: `0b0a637e5b000571` stands for the whole 256x240 screen, hashed by the colour of each pixel (`kind` `pixel`). The same screen gives the same 16 characters at any later stop.

gfx_view.what: Draw bytes of a ROM region or of memory as tiles, in a layout you state in MAME's `gfx_layout` terms.
gfx_view.ask: Show me sprite tiles 88 to 95 of Gridlee's graphics ROM in the palette's colours, starting at pen 832.
gfx_view.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped in attract mode. The example session's manifest, `docs/reference/tour/gridlee-gfx.yaml`, is loaded and names the format `sprite`.
gfx_view.reads: Tiles 88 to 95 of the 256 the region holds, 8 by 16 pixels at 4 bits a pixel. `real_colors` says they are drawn in the machine's own colours.

arguments.layout: The tile format: an object, a format name of the loaded `gfx.yaml` or a `gfx_sweep` candidate's id. An object has `width`, `height`, `planes`, `planeoffset`, `xoffset`, `yoffset` and `charincrement`, in bits.
arguments.palette: The colours: `none` for a grey ramp, a palette device's tag, or empty for the machine's only palette. Left out, `none`.
arguments.tag: The memory region or share to read, such as `gfx1`. Give this or `ref`, never both.
arguments.ref: An address or symbol in a cpu's memory where tile 0 starts, instead of `tag`. It needs `count`.
arguments.offset: Bytes into the `tag` block where tile 0 starts: an integer or a `0x` string. Not taken with `ref`.
arguments.first: The index of the first tile drawn. Left out, 0.
arguments.count: How many tiles to draw, at most 1024. 0 draws every tile the block holds, up to that many.
arguments.columns: Tiles in a row of the picture, 1 to 64. Left out, 16.
arguments.pen_base: The first pen of the palette the tiles are drawn with. It needs a `palette` other than `none`.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, up to 8. 0 picks the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new file the PNG is written to. Left empty, it goes to the session's temporary folder.
arguments.attach: `false` writes the picture without attaching it to the reply.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory `ref` is in. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing; not taken with `tag`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds.

returns.image: The PNG. It is indexed, and its index is the pixel value under any palette.
returns.tiles_available: How many whole tiles of this layout the block holds from the offset.
returns.real_colors: `false` under palette `none`: the greys are not the machine's colours.
returns.layout: The layout with every expression worked out to numbers, and its `name`.
returns.kind: Where the bytes came from: `region`, `share` or `space`, a cpu's memory. `tag`, `size`, `bytewidth`, `endianness` and `offset` describe it, and a `ref` adds `addr` and `addr_cpu`.

refuses: A `layout` that is not one, or one that uses `RGN_FRAC` with `ref` (`bad_argument`).
Both `tag` and `ref`, neither, or `ref` without `count` (`bad_argument`).
Tiles past the end of the block, or a palette with fewer pens than the depth needs, which is never padded (`bad_argument`).
More than 1048576 pixels in one call, or a block too large to read (`bad_argument`).
A tag, a palette or a format name that is not there (`unknown_ref`).
why: The layout is written in MAME's own `gfx_layout` terms, so a driver's layout copies over as it is. Its `total` becomes `first` and `count`, and plane 0 is the top bit. Those terms also state formats a bit depth cannot: byte-interleaved planes, planes a third of a region apart, packed nibbles, a linear framebuffer.
To try other colours, replace the palette inside the PNG: the tool takes a palette device, never a list of colours.

`tag` names a memory region, the ROM data MAME loads, or a share, RAM a driver names. A region is read whole, in the block's own byte order. A share is read a byte at a time, so the largest share it reads is smaller.
why_more: `RGN_FRAC` is a fraction of a block's length, and a range of a cpu's memory has no length of its own, so `ref` refuses it.

gfx_locate.what: Find which tile of a block is drawn in a patch of the screen, and so prove the tile format against the picture.
gfx_locate.ask: Which tile of the graphics ROM is the sprite at (148, 164) on screen, 8 by 16 pixels, with value 0 transparent?
gfx_locate.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped in attract mode with the player's sprite on screen. A `gfx_sweep` of the region `gfx1` has given the id `s1c1`.
gfx_locate.reads: One tile of the region equals the window on screen, and nothing else matched it (`ambiguous`). Which tile, with its flip and its palette base, is in `matches`, in the whole reply below.

arguments.layouts: A list of 1 to 8 formats to try, a list even for one. Each is a `gfx_view` layout or a `gfx_sweep` candidate's id such as `s1c3`.
arguments.patch: The rectangle of the screen to search, `[x, y, width, height]`. It must hold a whole tile.
arguments.tag: The memory region or share whose tiles are searched. Give this or `ref`.
arguments.ref: An address or symbol where tile 0 starts, instead of `tag`. It needs `count`.
arguments.offset: Bytes into the `tag` block where tile 0 starts: an integer or a `0x` string.
arguments.first: The index of the first tile tried. Left out, 0.
arguments.count: How many tiles are tried, up to 65536. 0 tries every tile the block holds.
arguments.transparent: A pixel value left out of the comparison, as for a sprite over a background. Left out, every pixel is compared.
arguments.flips: The flips tried, from `none`, `x`, `y` and `xy`. Left out, all four.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory `ref` is in. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of reading the screen and the block, in seconds. The search itself is not timed.

returns.matched: `true` when a tile equals a window of the patch pixel for pixel. `matches_total` counts the matches.
returns.matches: The first 32, each with `layout`, `window`, `tile`, `flip`, `base`, `bit`, `byte`, `compared`, `shape` and its own `ambiguous`.
returns.ambiguous: `true` when more than one tile or flip matched the same window. `ambiguous_windows` counts such windows.
returns.pen_map: Whether the second search ran (`tried`) and its `matches`, or `why` it did not.
returns.nearest: With no match, the closest miss: `layout`, `window`, `tile`, `flip`, `disagree` pixels out of `of`, the first `pixels` that differ, `is_a_match` and `complete`.

refuses: A `patch` that leaves the screen or holds no whole tile of any layout (`bad_argument`).
A search larger than one call does, or a pattern repeated so often that its matches tell nothing apart (`bad_argument`).
A screen drawn in direct colour, which holds no pens to search for (`no_channel`).
Whatever `gfx_view` refuses of a layout or of `tag`, `ref`, `offset` and `cpu`.
why: `gfx_view` draws bytes in a format you state, and nothing there says the format is right. A match here does: a tile whose pixels are exactly the pens on screen proves the format, where the tile sits in the block and its palette bank together. Each pixel must equal `base` plus the tile's value, exactly.

A `window` is a tile-sized rectangle of the patch, named by its top-left corner, and every one is tried against every tile. A window of one pen matches every blank tile, so it is counted and skipped. With one bit a pixel, sparse or symmetric glyphs match more than the tile drawn there, hence `ambiguous` and `flips`.

Nothing is ranked. Each answer is kept for `gfx_draft`, and `evidence` gives its number in the session's record. `shape` is the window's distinct rows, distinct columns and rarest pen's pixels, by which `gfx_draft` rules out a chance match.
why_more: A board can draw a tile's ink and paper from two palette banks, or show one value in two pens, and then no window is `base` plus value. So when the first search matches nothing, a second tries a table from each pen of the window to the value it stands for.

That table must give each pen one value and read at least two, since a tile of one value proves nothing. Its match proves the format and the tile, never the palette bank: it carries `pen_map` and no `base`.

With `transparent`, a match needs two different values among the pixels compared. A one-bit tile has one, so it matches only through the pen table, and proves its shape only when the ink's pens appear nowhere among the pixels left out.
`nearest` goes by the smallest share of disagreeing pixels, never their count, which would favour the smallest tile. Each of its `pixels` is `[x, y, screen pen, decoded value]`.

gfx_sweep.what: Draw a block of unknown format under a set of candidate layouts on one labelled sheet, to pick the one that looks like graphics.
gfx_sweep.ask: I don't know the format of Gridlee's sprite ROM: draw its first 16 tiles as 4-bit 8 by 16 candidates on one sheet.
gfx_sweep.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped in attract mode. `gfx1` is the region that holds its sprites.
gfx_sweep.reads: Three arrangements of 4 bits a pixel were drawn, each with an id the next call can take, such as `s1c1`. `real_colors` is false: the greys are not the game's colours.

arguments.tag: The memory region or share to draw. Give this or `ref`.
arguments.ref: An address or symbol in a cpu's memory to draw from, instead of `tag`.
arguments.offset: Bytes into the `tag` block where the tiles start: an integer or a `0x` string.
arguments.count: How many tiles each cell of the sheet shows, 1 to 64. Left out, 32.
arguments.planes: The bit depths to try, each 1 to 8. Left out, 1, 2 and 4.
arguments.sizes: The tile sizes to try, each `[width, height]` with sides of 8, 16, 24 or 32. Left out, 8 by 8.
arguments.palette: The colours: `none` for a grey ramp, a palette device's tag, or empty for the machine's only palette. Left out, `none`.
arguments.pen_base: The first pen the tiles are drawn with, under a palette other than `none`.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the sheet is enlarged by, up to 8. 0 picks the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new file the sheet is written to. Left empty, it goes to the session's temporary folder.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory `ref` is in. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds.

returns.candidates: One row per layout tried: its `id` such as `s1c3`, `what` it is in words, its `tiles_available` and how many are `shown`.
returns.sweep: The number of this sheet in the session, the first half of each candidate's id.
returns.image: The sheet, each cell labelled with its id and its layout.
returns.cell_scale: The factor the tiles inside each cell are enlarged by.
returns.next: The two calls that take an id from this sheet, written out.
returns.real_colors: `false` under palette `none`: the greys are not the machine's colours.

refuses: More than 16 candidates: narrow `planes` or `sizes` (`bad_argument`).
A block that holds no whole tile of any candidate, or a sheet too large to attach (`bad_argument`).
Both `tag` and `ref`, or neither (`bad_argument`).
A tag or a palette the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
why: A board nobody has described has no format to state, and a format must not be guessed. So the block is drawn under every arrangement MAME's layouts are made of, side by side, and you pick the cell that looks like graphics.

Nothing ranks the cells: a ranking that looks like proof is worse than an honest list. A candidate's id is a layout for `gfx_view` and for `gfx_locate`, which checks it against the screen. `gfx_draft(choose=...)` records your pick.
The set of candidates is fixed and never tuned to a board. Give `planes` or `sizes` only when you know them.
why_more: Each candidate is a depth, a tile size, a pixel order and, past one plane, a plane arrangement, in the words `what` uses. Candidates with the same offsets are drawn once.

| in `what` | meaning |
|---|---|
| `rows` | pixels row by row |
| `cells across` | a tile of several 8x8 cells, across and then down |
| `cells down` | the cells down and then across |
| `packed` | a pixel's bits together, plane 0 the top bit |
| `planar` | the planes' bytes of each 8-pixel group in turn |
| `split` | each plane a fraction of the block apart: `tag` only |

gfx_draft.what: Write a draft `gfx.yaml` from what this session's `gfx_locate` answers and your picks proved, with a report of every figure beside it.
gfx_draft.ask: Write down what we worked out about Gridlee's sprite format as a draft manifest, and record that the tour picked candidate s1c1.
gfx_draft.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, after the `gfx_sweep` and `gfx_locate` calls shown on this page. The pick of `s1c1` is recorded as the example session's.
gfx_draft.reads: The one format written is the recorded pick, marked `human`: `not_proved` says the match found here proves no layout. No asset is written, since the pick was made under no palette.

arguments.dest: An absolute `.yaml` path in an existing folder, where only an earlier draft is replaced. Left empty, the session's temporary folder.
arguments.choose: Records a person's pick from a `gfx_sweep` sheet before drafting: `{"candidate": "s1c3", "chosen_by": "<who>"}`.

returns.manifest: The draft: its `path` and `sha256`. `report` gives the same two for the JSON report.
returns.formats: Each format written, by name, with its status: `proved` or `human`.
returns.not_proved: The first 8 things the session could not settle, in words. `not_proved_more` counts the rest.
returns.evidence: What the draft was worked out from: how many `locates`, `sweeps`, `choices` and `correlations`.
returns.confirm: How the draft becomes a manifest: delete its first line.

refuses: A session with no `gfx_locate` answer and no pick (`needs_call`).
A `dest` that exists and is not a draft, so a confirmed manifest is never overwritten (`bad_argument`).
A `dest` that is not a `.yaml` file, or a `choose` of another shape (`bad_argument`).
A `dest` holding a space, comma, semicolon, quote, bracket or control character, although no console line carries that file: one rule serves every path (`bad_argument`).
A `choose` that names no candidate of this session's sheets (`unknown_ref`).
why: The draft holds only what the session's record establishes: every `gfx_locate` answer, every `gfx_sweep` sheet and every pick, kept until `close` or the next `start`. Each entry is written with its status and what proved it. What the record cannot settle is listed in `not_proved`.

A format is `proved` by a match whose window varies along both axes and whose rarest pen covers the tile's longer side. No other block may match those pixels on the same frame, since a pixel has one origin. A dot or a line is found by chance among hundreds of tiles.

The draft's first line marks it as a draft, and deleting that line confirms it. `gfx_load` takes it before that and says `draft: true`, so a draw command the draft found can be tried with `gfx_blits` first.
why_more: A match is only as strong as the search is wide, and you set the width. A patch cut to one window matches once whenever it matches, so the number of windows tried says nothing; the rarest pen does. At three planes or more, a layout's only match in a search of every tile also proves it.

Two layouts of one tile size that both matched are rivals. One is proved only when an answer that tried both saw it match a window the other missed; otherwise neither is written. Layouts of different sizes are not rivals.

A pick from a `gfx_sweep` sheet is written as `human` where nothing of its tile size is proved. A match that proves the same layout turns it into `proved`, and a match that proves another is reported as contradicting it.
An asset is written for each block and palette bank a format was drawn with; `asset_names` lists them. A format matched only through `gfx_locate`'s pen table proves no bank, so it gets no asset.

A draw command comes from a capture watch (`watch_add`), paired with the answers whose matches all sit in one window. An answer of screen frame F pairs with the capture's row of frame F minus a lag. Each word of the block is tried as `dest_x`, `dest_y` and `source_tile`, with a sign and an `add`.
A capture whose callbacks raised is short of writes, so the draft proves no draw command from it and says why in `not_proved`.

A reading holds when it agrees on every paired answer, on enough of them, with a value that changes. The lag is the one at which both x and y hold; none or several settle nothing. A role that holds only at another lag is left out and named (`elsewhere`); `command_fields` lists what was written.

Every figure lives in the report, which the same record regenerates byte for byte, and the draft's `source` lines name the report's key. A `choose` is recorded once however often it is made, and not at all when the draft fails.

gfx_blits.what: Show every draw (blit) a board made in one frame as a box over the screen, coloured by the code that issued it.
gfx_blits.ask: Which code drew over the rectangle at (148, 164), 8 by 16 pixels, in frame 545?
gfx_blits.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, with the example session's manifest loaded. A capture watch on the player's sprite entry (`0xc`, 4 bytes, trigger `0x10`) has recorded two frames.
gfx_blits.reads: One blit covers the area, issued from `write_sprites+0x29`, whose boxes are drawn in `#ff4040`. `topmost` names it as the likeliest painter; its `n` is the capture's row, and it has no plane because the command names none.

arguments.draw_command: The name of a draw command in the loaded `gfx.yaml`, whose register block a capture watch is recording.
arguments.frame: The frame whose blits are shown. Left out, the newest frame before this stop that has any.
arguments.area: A rectangle of the screen, `[x, y, width, height]`. The reply then lists the blits covering it, in the order drawn.
arguments.detail: `true` lists every blit of the frame, 24 a page.
arguments.first: The first blit of the list to show, for the next page. It needs `area` or `detail`.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, up to 8. 0 picks the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new file the PNG is written to. Left empty, it goes to the session's temporary folder.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds.

returns.frame_blit: The frame shown. `frame_complete` is `false` when this stop is still inside it or rows were lost.
returns.legend: One row per writer: its `pc`, its `symbol`, the `color` of its boxes and how many `blits` it made.
returns.by_plane: The blits by `plane` and `page`: how many `blits`, and how many are `on_screen`.
returns.topmost: With `area`, the last covering blit of the highest plane: its `index`, `n` (the capture's row), `pc` and `plane`.
returns.blits: With `area` or `detail`, a page of blits: `index`, `n`, `pc`, `box`, `plane`, `page`, the `screen` rectangles, `on_screen`, `clipped`, `fields` and `flags`.
returns.not_proved: The fields and planes of the command this answer relied on whose status in the manifest is not `proved`.

refuses: No manifest loaded (`needs_call`), or a command it does not have (`unknown_ref`).
No capture watch on the command's block; `declare` gives the `watch_add` call that sets one (`bad_argument`).
A capture that was never installed, or one with no rows yet (`bad_argument`).
A frame with no blit, or one past the rows the capture kept (`bad_argument`).
Captures on two cpus for a command whose `block` names none (`bad_argument`).
An `area` off the screen, or a `first` past the list (`bad_argument`).
why: Covering is not painting. A box says where a blit's destination lands; what painted a pixel also depends on the source pixels, their transparency and any scaling, which the rows do not carry. So `topmost` is the likeliest painter, not a proven one.

The tool reads rows a capture watch already recorded and never sets one itself: a watch set behind your back would change the run. With none, the refusal gives the `watch_add` call to make, and the rows start at the next run.

The reply is a summary by default, because every blit of a frame with every field would not fit a reply. Ask for an `area` or for `detail`, and page with the same `frame`: a finished frame's rows do not change.
why_more: A capture keeps its rows in order and drops every row past its limit. Only the last kept frame can have lost some, and it says `rows_cut`.

A box is the destination rectangle wrapped at its plane's size, moved by the plane's origin read from the same row, and cut to the screen. On a plane drawn in pages each blit names its `page`; which page the screen shows is not in the rows.
The picture is RGB, the screen's colours with the boxes over them: a view of the data. `screen_view` gives the pens themselves. A listed blit that covers no pixel says `why`.

gfx_blit_source.what: Show the rectangle of graphics one blit reads, decoded from the command's asset with the live palette, always unscaled.
gfx_blit_source.ask: Show me the graphics the first blit of the newest frame reads from its source.
gfx_blit_source.on: This tool needs a board whose draw command states where in the source each blit reads; neither free program has one. The reply shown comes from a test program that is not distributed.
gfx_blit_source.reads: The first blit of frame 6 reads a 2 by 1 rectangle at (22, 11) of tile 0 of the asset `pages`. `reads_source` is true: the manifest says this blit does read its source.

arguments.draw_command: The name of a draw command in the loaded `gfx.yaml`, as for `gfx_blits`.
arguments.frame: The frame the blit belongs to. Left out, the newest frame before this stop that has blits.
arguments.index: The blit's order in its frame, as `gfx_blits` lists it. Give this or `pc`.
arguments.pc: The address or symbol of the code that issued the blit, instead of `index`. It must have issued one blit in the frame.
arguments.margin: Pixels of context shown round the rectangle, 0 to 16, dimmed. Left out, none.
arguments.scale: The whole factor the picture is enlarged by, up to 8. 0 picks the largest that fits.
arguments.dest: A new file the PNG is written to. Left empty, it goes to the session's temporary folder.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read, in seconds.

returns.rect: What the blit reads: the `tile`, the `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` inside it, and the directions `dir_x` and `dir_y`.
returns.image: The picture. With a `margin` it is a view: the context dimmed, the rectangle ringed in white.
returns.data: With a `margin`, the exact indexed PNG of the whole window, each pixel its value.
returns.box: Where the rectangle sits inside the picture: `[x, y, width, height]`.
returns.reads_source: `false` when the manifest says this blit reads no source. The rectangle is then where its registers point, not what it drew.
returns.not_proved: The command's fields this answer relied on whose status in the manifest is not `proved`.

refuses: Whatever `gfx_blits` refuses of the manifest, the capture or the frame.
A command with no `asset`, or without the `source_x` and `source_y` roles (`bad_argument`).
Both `index` and `pc`, or neither (`bad_argument`).
A `pc` that issued no blit in the frame, or several; `indexes` lists them (`bad_argument`).
A tile past the asset's block, or a rectangle that leaves a tile whose asset does not wrap (`bad_argument`).
A `pc` symbol the session does not know (`unknown_ref`).
why: The picture is unscaled on purpose. A blit drawn enlarged or shrunk reads another extent of the source, and how a board scales is that project's rule, which is not applied here. The rectangle is the size of the destination, taken from the source origin.

A `margin` is dimmed because, drawn like the rectangle, its pixels would read as part of the blit: an offset that does not exist. That view is RGB, since an indexed file cannot dim a pen without a second palette entry, which a board using all 256 pens does not have.
why_more: The rectangle is decoded with the tile's own layout, its offsets narrowed to the rectangle, which is exact for every layout MAME's layout terms can state. The origin carries each field's `add` from the manifest, and the rectangle wraps inside the tile when the asset says `wrap`.

gfx_load.what: Load a project's `gfx.yaml`, the file that names its tile formats, graphics assets, draw commands and palette ports for the other tools.
gfx_load.ask: Load the graphics manifest this repository keeps for Gridlee.
gfx_load.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, at any stop. The manifest is the example session's, `docs/reference/tour/gridlee-gfx.yaml` in this repository.
gfx_load.reads: One format and one asset, and all nine entries of the file are `proved`. The asset `sprites` reads the region `gfx1` in the format `sprite`, with the palette device `palette`.

arguments.path: The absolute path of the `gfx.yaml`. A load replaces the one before.

returns.draft: `true` when the first line is `gfx_draft`'s draft marker. Deleting that line confirms the draft.
returns.formats: Each format's name with its status.
returns.commands: Each draw command: its `block` address and `length`, its `trigger_addr` and the value it `fires_with`, its `asset`, `roles`, `flags` and `planes`.

refuses: An unknown or missing key, a wrong type or a name that points at nothing; the message gives its full path (`bad_argument`).
YAML outside the subset the reader takes; the message names the line (`bad_argument`).
A manifest whose `systems` does not list the session's system (`bad_argument`).
A `path` that is not absolute (`bad_argument`).
why: The file is checked whole, so a half-loaded manifest never answers a later call. A misspelt key is refused with its full path, such as `commands.blit.fields.dest_x.parts[1].maks`, because a key silently ignored is a setting silently left at its default. A refusal keeps the previous load and names it in `still_loaded`.

A manifest states what a project knows, and nothing in it runs; it loads while the program runs too. It holds no measured figure, which would go out of date there: a figure belongs in the report or the commit that measured it.

The reader takes a subset of YAML and refuses a value another YAML reader could type differently: `no`, `012`, `1e3`, a date, `1:20`. Quote such a value. Anchors, tags, block scalars, tabs and duplicate keys are outside the subset.
why_more: The format of a `gfx.yaml`, as a small manifest that loads:

```yaml
schema: 1
systems: [myboard]                 # the MAME systems it describes
formats:
  chars:
    layout:                        # as gfx_view takes one
      width: 8
      height: 8
      planes: 1
      planeoffset: [0]
      xoffset: '{ STEP8(0,1) }'
      yoffset: '{ STEP8(0,8) }'
      charincrement: 8*8
    status: declared
    source: myboard.cpp charlayout
assets:
  font: {format: chars, tag: gfx1, palette: palette, status: declared, source: myboard.cpp}
commands:
  blit:
    # the registers a capture watch records, and the write that makes a row a blit
    block: {address: 0x700000, words: 16, word_bytes: 2, status: declared, source: myboard.cpp}
    fire: {word: 15, value: 0xffff, status: declared, source: myboard.cpp}
    asset: font
    fields:                        # the roles the server computes with
      dest_x:
        parts:
          - {word: 0, mask: 0x00ff}
          - {word: 7, mask: 0x0040, at: 8}
        status: proved
        source: the boxes checked against the screen
      dest_y: {parts: [{word: 2, mask: 0x00ff}], status: declared, source: myboard.cpp}
      width: {const: 8, status: declared, source: myboard.cpp}
      height: {const: 8, status: declared, source: myboard.cpp}
palette_ports:
  ramdac:
    palette: palette
    index_port: 0x720001
    data_port: 0x720003
    order: [r, g, b]
    component_bits: 8
    auto_increment: true
    status: declared
    source: myboard.cpp
```

An asset may add `offset`, `pen_base` and `wrap`, for coordinates that wrap inside a tile. A command's `block` may name its `cpu`. Its `fire` is a `word` of the block with a `value`, or an `address` outside the block; with no `value`, every write there fires.

The roles are `dest_x`, `dest_y`, then `dest_x_end` and `dest_y_end` (inclusive) or `width` and `height`; `dest_dir_x`, `dest_dir_y`; `source_x`, `source_y`, `source_tile`, `source_dir_x`, `source_dir_y`; `plane`; `reads_source`. Anything else to show goes under `flags`, read the same way and never interpreted.

A field is a list of `parts`: each takes the bits of `mask` from one `word`, low bit first, and puts them from bit `at` of the value. An optional `add` is added, and `sign: -1` reads a value stored reversed. A fixed size is a `const`, and a one-bit role says with `asserted` which value means it holds.

A command's `planes` each have a `name` and the `width` and `height` they wrap at. One is picked by the `plane` role's value (`when`), and a higher `order` is drawn over a lower. `origin_x` and `origin_y` are an integer or `{field, scale, add}` read from the blit's own row, and `page` names the field that says which page.
A `palette_ports` entry may add `cpu`, `space` (`program` or `io`), `pen_base`, `pen_count` and `protocol`; `component_bits` is 1 to 8. Two entries on one palette may not set the same pens.

`protocol` is `ramdac` (the default), `latch`, which needs `index_flag_mask` and may leave `index_port` out, or `sequence`. The last two may set `components_bit_reversed`. `pen_count` is a power of two up to 1024, and always 256 for `ramdac`.
A section named `ramdacs` is read as `palette_ports`, and `note` says so. The reply also carries the file's `sha256` and its `systems`.

gfx_film.what: Keep a picture of each frame in which a chosen write happened, and read them back as one contact sheet.
gfx_film.ask: Keep a picture of every frame in the next 90 where the game writes its credits, two pictures at most.
gfx_film.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped in attract mode with the example session's symbols loaded, so `credits` names the byte that counts coins.

then.lead: Then, after a coin and those 90 frames, read the film:

gfx_film.reads: The film waits to be installed, then checks 90 frames (`judged`). One of them held a write to `credits` (`met`), and its picture was kept.

arguments.trigger: The address or symbol whose write is watched. Giving it arms the film, with the program stopped; left empty, the call reads the film.
arguments.length: How many bytes the write covers: 1, 2 or 4. Left out, 1.
arguments.value: Only a write of this value counts: an integer or a `0x` string. Not taken with `changed`.
arguments.changed: `true` counts only a write whose value differs from the one before.
arguments.pc: Only a write made from this address or symbol counts.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory `trigger` is in. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.frames: How many frames the film checks before it finishes, up to 216000. Left out, 600.
arguments.keep: How many pictures it keeps, up to 64. Left out, 12.
arguments.crop: The rectangle of the screen each picture keeps, `[x, y, width, height]`. Left out, the whole screen.
arguments.film_dir: A new absolute folder for the film's files. Left empty, a new folder in the session's temporary folder.
arguments.first: When reading, the first kept frame the sheet shows, counted from 0.
arguments.clear: `true` removes the film. Its files stay.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the read that arms the film, in seconds. Reading the sheet is not timed.
arguments.space: `io` when `trigger` is an I/O port. Left out, `program`, the cpu's memory.

returns.armed_now: `true` on the call that arms the film. It starts at the first whole frame after it is installed.
returns.film: What the film was armed with, and `checked`: whether each kept frame is compared with MAME's own rendering.
returns.state: When reading: `judging` while frames are still being checked, then `finished`. Before any result it is `no_dump_yet`, `install_failed` or `install_lost`, with `why`.
returns.met: How many of the `judged` frames held the write. `kept` counts the pictures kept and `refused` those that failed their check.
returns.cells: One row per kept frame on this page: `k`, `frame`, `hits_in_frame`, `hit_counters`, the first hit's `pc`, `symbol` and `value`, and the picture's `path`.
returns.image: The contact sheet of this page, once a frame is kept. `next_first` starts the next page.

refuses: Arming while the program runs (`not_stopped`); reading and clearing need no stop.
A second film while one is armed: one a session (`bad_argument`).
A read with no film armed (`needs_call`).
`value` together with `changed`, or an argument that arming, reading or clearing does not take (`bad_argument`).
A `trigger` whose `length` bytes cross a bus word: one bus write must cover them (`bad_argument`).
A `first` past the kept frames, or a `crop` off the screen (`bad_argument`).
why: A breakpoint cannot follow a write that happens many times a frame. So the film runs inside MAME at full speed: a hook on the write marks the frame, and at the frame's end only a marked frame has its picture kept.

A register a game writes every frame meets a fixed `value` on nearly every frame, which records everything and filters nothing. `changed` is the question a film is usually asked. Its `pc` filter applies to the write, not to the value it is compared with, and a reset or a state load starts no new comparison.

A write made during vblank belongs to this frame's picture, yet MAME's frame counter still reads the frame before. So each hit keeps the counter it read. A row joins `gfx_blits(frame=...)` and a capture's rows by `hit_counters`, never by `frame`, which names the picture.
why_more: Each picture is read one frame late, at the next frame's end. MAME turns the screen's double buffer over before its frame notifiers run, so one of them reads the frame that ended only after the next turn. That rule says nothing about a read at a debugger stop, which [Screen](screen.md) covers.
With frameskip the buffer turns only on a frame that was drawn, so a frame that held the write and was skipped is counted in `lost`.

Where MAME's snapshot is the bare screen, each kept frame is compared with it pixel for pixel, and one that differs is refused with no picture. `refused_frames` gives each one's `k`, `code` and `why`.

Elsewhere the film says `checked: false`, and `mismatch` measures how the snapshot differed at the stop where the film was armed. It asserts no cause: its `candidates` names the one its rule leaves standing.

| in `candidates` | when |
|---|---|
| `orientation` | a mirrored screen equals the snapshot |
| `frame_lag` | no mirror, and every differing pixel is in a pen's colour |
| `colour_adjustment` | each screen colour is drawn as one snapshot colour, no two alike |
| `overlay_or_artwork` | anything else, and a snapshot of another size, where nothing is compared |

A `start` does not arm the film again. A film spends its frames and pictures from the moment it is armed, and a new start would spend them on the boot. `clear` keeps the files, and a later film writes into a folder of its own.

- `frame-K.png`: one per kept frame.
- `film.json`: every kept frame with its file, `sha256`, check, `hits_in_frame`, `hit_counters` and first hits, and every refused one with its reason.
- `sheet-F.png`: one per page read.
- `film-anim.png`: every kept frame as an animation, never attached.
`cost` is the frame notifier's own host time inside MAME; the hook's cost per write is not in it.
A film whose callbacks raised says so in `nothing_kept` when it kept no picture: frames that met the condition may not have been marked.

palette_log.what: Find which code set a pen's colour on a board whose palette cannot be read back, by logging every write to its palette ports.
palette_log.ask: Start logging every write to this board's palette ports, so I can ask later which code set a pen.
palette_log.on: This tool needs a board that sets its colours through ports; Gridlee's are fixed in PROMs, and neither free program has such a board. The reply shown comes from a test program that is not distributed.
palette_log.reads: The log is armed on the two ports of the entry `ramdac`, an index port and a data port. It is not installed yet (`pending`): that happens when the console next reads a line, and it records from there.

arguments.palette_port: The name of an entry under `palette_ports` in the loaded `gfx.yaml`.
arguments.pen: Show this pen alone: its state and the rows that wrote it. Left out, the reply lists the writers of every pen.
arguments.limit: How many of the newest rows the reply shows, 0 to 256. Left out, 16.
arguments.arm: `true` starts the log. Without it the call reads the log, and never starts one.

returns.installed: `false` on the call that arms it. The log is installed when the console next reads a line, at a step or the next frame run, and records from there.
returns.state: Once armed: `logged` when there is a table to read. Otherwise `no_dump_yet`, `install_failed` or `install_lost`, with `why`.
returns.writes_total: Every write the log saw. `unsynced_writes` landed while the device's index was not known, and `desyncs` counts the times it was lost.
returns.setters: Without `pen`, the first 32 writers, most pens first: `pc`, `symbol`, `written_by`, how many `pens_set` and `which`. `setters_path` holds them all.
returns.pen_state: With `pen`: its `color`, whether it is `complete`, its `components`, its `writes_total` and the `last` write.
returns.rows: The newest `limit` rows in order, each with `n`, `frame`, `pc`, `written_by`, the screen `line`, `time_s`, and the `pen`, `component`, `value` and `color` it left.

refuses: No manifest loaded, or a read with no log armed; the message gives the call that arms it (`needs_call`).
A `palette_port` the manifest does not have (`unknown_ref`).
A `pen` the entry does not set (`bad_argument`).
`arm` with `clear`, or `pen` or `limit` with either (`bad_argument`).
A log armed from an entry the manifest has since changed: clear it and arm it again (`needs_call`).
