why: A RAMDAC takes an index on one port and the colour's components one after another on a second port, so a data write names no pen. Which pen it landed on is known only by following the device from its last index write, which the log does inside MAME with the rule of MAME's own `ramdac_device`.

Until the first index write after arming, a reset or a state load, the index is not known. A write then counts in `unsynced_writes` and is given to no pen, because a guessed index is a plausible wrong pen.

`written_by` is `guest` for the program, or `debugger` for a write made while the machine stood in the debugger, whose `pc` is where the machine stood and not a writer. Rows carry the screen `line` being drawn and `time_s`, so a palette write in the middle of a frame can be ordered against another cpu's captured writes.
why_more: A stop asked for from outside is requested before the cpu reaches the instruction it stops at, so the program's last instruction still counts as `guest`. Every call of this tool answers while the program runs.

The other two protocols put a whole colour in one word, read little-endian from the port up to the end of its bus word. A big-endian bus, or an index port inside the data port's bus word, fails when the log is installed (`install_failed`).

`latch`: a data word with a bit of `index_flag_mask` set sets the index to its low bits; any other word is the indexed pen's colour, written whole. A write to `index_port` merges into the index under its mask. While the index is unknown, only a write covering every index bit makes it known.
`sequence`: each data write merges into the stored word of the pen at the current offset, under its mask. Any write to `index_port`'s bus word sets the offset back to 0.
A driver that zeroes that offset as its video starts leaves a log armed right after `start` knowing it (`synced_at_start`). Armed anywhere else, the log waits for a write a game may never make again.

In both, a pen has a colour only once every colour bit of its word has been seen written. A write that merges into bits the log never saw counts in `partial_writes`, and the pen has no colour until they are.
A row of an index write carries `index`, and one of a whole-colour write `word` and `mask`. A row that landed on no pen says `unsynced`; one where the index was lost says `desync` and `why`.

A log whose callbacks raised carries `callback_errors`, with their `count` and the `first` error, and a pen with no write logged then says one may have been missed. A log whose periodic write to disk keeps failing shows its last finished table, and `why` gives the error.

scan.what: Find the byte that holds a value nobody has named: start from a whole range and keep only what changes as the value does.
scan.ask: Find the byte where this game counts its credits: scan the first 2 KB and filter after each of three coins.
scan.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, five seconds after power-on. The demo drops three coins and filters after each; these are its first call and its last.
scan.reads: Three bytes still hold 3 after three coins. Two of them, `0x42b` and `0x42c`, are the credits, which the game keeps twice.

head: method
what it does
rows: Opens a scan: every cell of the range is a candidate.
Keeps the candidates whose value passes a comparison.

arguments.ref: Where the range begins, for `start`: a `0x` address or a symbol.
arguments.length: How many bytes to scan, for `start`: at most `0x100000`.
arguments.cell_bytes: The size of each candidate: 1, 2 or 4 bytes. Left out, one byte.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose program memory is scanned. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.operator: The comparison a `filter` makes. Left out, `=`.
arguments.value: What each candidate is compared with: an integer or a `0x` string. Left out, what it held at `start`.
arguments.limit: How many of the candidates left the reply lists: 1 to 400. Left out, 40.

returns.hits: The first `limit` of them, each with its address and its value now.
returns.iterations: How many filters this scan has taken.
returns.closed: `true` when a filter left no candidate, which ends the scan.
returns.truncated: `true` when there are more candidates than `hits` lists.

refuses: An argument the method does not take.
A second `start` while a scan is open, or a `filter` with none (`needs_call`).
A range that runs past the cpu's program memory (`bad_argument`).
why: The scan reads memory the way the cpu does, through the board's own handlers, so it sees what MAME's cheat search cannot. It belongs to one cpu, because every filter must read the same memory.
One scan is open at a time, and nothing you do between filters ends it: running, writing, a reset or loading a saved state. That is what lets a coin go in between two filters.

write.what: Write bytes into memory at an address or a symbol, and see what the memory holds afterwards.
write.ask: Give me nine credits: write 9 into both bytes the game keeps its credits in.
write.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, at any stop, with the example session's symbols loaded: `credits` names the first of the two bytes the game keeps its credits in.
write.reads: Both bytes from `0x42b` now hold 9. `readback` is what the memory holds after the write, and `verified` says it is what was sent.

arguments.ref: Where the bytes go: a `0x` address or a symbol.
arguments.data_hex: The bytes to write, as hex digits, two per byte: 1 to 1024 bytes.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose memory is written. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.region: `true` patches ROM, in the memory region that holds the address. Left out, a write to ROM changes nothing and the reply says why.

returns.readback: The bytes at the address after the write, as hex, read through the same cpu.
returns.bytes_written: How many bytes were sent, whether or not they landed.
returns.target: `rom`, when a write without `region` did not land because the address is ROM. `note` then says where its bytes live.
returns.region: The memory region that holds the address, with `region_offset` the offset in it: where a `region` write went, or where a ROM address keeps its bytes.
returns.captures_reading_it: With `region`: each capture watch that reads the block the write changed, by `ref`, `cpu` and, for a port, `space`.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
`data_hex` that is not whole hex bytes, is empty, or holds more than 1024 (`bad_argument`).
A range that runs past the cpu's program memory (`bad_argument`).
`region=true` where no memory region holds the address, or where the bytes run past its end (`bad_argument`).
A `cpu` other than the first, on a MAME build whose debugger connection serves one cpu only (`bad_argument`).
A failed read after the write, with the session still usable (`readback_refused`) or not (`session_broken`).
why: The reply says what the memory holds after the write, never what was sent. A write to ROM is taken and changes nothing, and `readback` is where that shows. `verified: false` on RAM means the write went nowhere; on a hardware register it can be the register answering something else, which is its job.

ROM is patched only with `region`, so it never happens by accident. As the cpu sees it ROM has no write side: its bytes live in a memory region, and `region=true` changes them there without running an instruction.
The write marks the session: the `session` block of every later reply carries `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine.
why_more: A capture watch, `watch_add(mode="capture")`, records a block of memory each time its trigger address is accessed. A `region` write changes that block with no write on the bus, so the watch would show the change with nothing saying why; the reply names each watch it reaches.

With `region`, `data_hex` is still in the order the cpu reads the bytes, whatever order the region keeps them in. The write lands whole or not at all: when the console cannot copy the whole span out and back, it is refused and nothing is loaded.

set_register.what: Force a register to a value you choose, and see what the cpu holds afterwards.
set_register.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, at any stop.
set_register.reads: Register A of `:maincpu` now holds `0x42`. `readback` is what the register held after the write, and `verified` says it equals what was asked.

arguments.name: The register, by a name `registers` lists (`D0`, `PC`). A 16-bit register served under an `E` name takes its short one: `AX` for `EAX` on a V30.
arguments.value: The value to set: an integer or a `0x` string, not negative and no wider than the register.
arguments.cpu: The cpu whose register is set. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.

returns.register: The register as the debugger names it, which can differ from the name given (`EAX` for `AX`).
returns.value: What was asked, as `0x` text at the register's width.
returns.readback: What the register holds after the write, in the same spelling.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A name the cpu does not have; the message lists the ones it has (`bad_argument`).
A negative value, or one wider than the register (`bad_argument`).
A bool, or a value of either spelling wider than 64 bits, the widest number MAME's debugger holds (`bad_argument`).
A `cpu` other than the first, on a MAME build whose debugger connection serves one cpu only (`bad_argument`).
A cpu whose registers the debugger connection does not describe (`no_channel`).
why: The value is read back because a register can refuse part of it. `verified: false` is not always a failure: a register that masks the value, or answers something else, is doing its job.
The write marks the session: the `session` block of every later reply carries `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine.

reset.what: Soft-reset the machine without restarting MAME, and stop where its boot begins.
reset.ask: Reset the game without restarting MAME.
reset.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, at any stop. The example session resets at frame 630, with a game under way.
reset.reads: The machine is back at `0xf000`, the address `start` first stopped it at, so `verified` is true. The frame counter did not restart: `frame_at_reset` is 630.

returns.kind: Always `softreset`: the only reset this tool makes.
returns.pc: Where the machine is after the reset.
returns.boot_pc: Where `start` left the machine at boot. Unavailable when `start` read no address then.
returns.verified: `true` when `pc` and `boot_pc` agree: the machine is back where it boots.
returns.frame_at_reset: The frame counter at the reset. It does not restart, so subtract this before comparing a frame with a fresh start's.
returns.taps_across: Each count or capture that was running across the reset, by `ref`, `cpu` and, for a port, `space`. Its totals carry on.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: The reset is a stop of its own: MAME applies it only when the machine next runs, so the call steps one instruction. That stop is recorded with the readings every stop returns, described on the [Run](run.md) page.

There is no hard reset: it re-creates the machine and ends the debugger connection, which is `close` then `start`. It would save only MAME's launch, none of the emulated time to the screen that matters.
A reset is a write: the `session` block of every later reply carries `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine.
why_more: A count or capture watch counts on across a reset, because its tables live outside the machine. For a fresh count, `declaration_clear(kind="watch")` and add the watch again.

debug.what: Send one line to MAME's debugger console and read what it printed, for what no other tool does.
debug.ask: Ask MAME's debugger what handles address 0x9380.
debug.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, at any stop.
debug.reads: `output` holds what the console's `map` command printed, shown here cut short: the whole reply below has it all. `mutates` is false: the line changed nothing.

arguments.command: One line for the debugger console, as you would type it there. Several commands go on one line, with `;` between them.

returns.output: What the console printed. Past 4000 characters it is cut: `clipped` is `true` and `output_path` names a file with all `output_chars` of it.
returns.mutates: `true` when the line can change the machine: it then counts as a write.
returns.note: What the line did beyond printing: it let the machine run, completed a held save or load, or moved a counter.
returns.visible_cpu: After a line that changes which cpus the debugger shows or skips: the cpu it shows now. `ignored` lists the ones it skips.
returns.refused: On a refusal: each command the console refused, with its `index` in the line, the `command` and the console's `error`. `not_run` lists the commands that never ran.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A line holding `hardreset`, before anything is sent: `close` then `start` is that reset (`bad_argument`).
A line the console answers with an error of its own, such as an unknown command or a bad expression (`bad_argument`).
A line too long for one packet of the debugger connection, before it is sent; `command_chars` and `limit_chars` say by how much (`bad_argument`).
A `statesave` or `stateload` MAME still holds after one instruction (`not_settled`).
why: A line that can change the machine counts as a write, whether it fills memory, loads a file, resets, runs or assigns a value. It marks the session: the `session` block of every later reply carries `altered`, which says this session has written to the machine.
A line that lets the machine run (`g` and its family, `step N`, `over`, `next`) leaves the session running until `stop`, and tools that read the machine refuse until then.
The console has no exit code, so its error answers are read. Otherwise a refused line would come back `ok`, and a `perform`, which runs several calls as one, would go on to its next step.
why_more: Each command is classified from MAME's own command table, on the cautious side. The cases that are not obvious:

- `suspend` and `resume` count when they name a cpu, and so does `source`, which runs a file of console commands.
- A bare `suspend`, `resume`, `ignore` or `observe` only lists.
- An action given to `bp`, `ep`, `rp`, `wp`, `trace` or `traceover` counts: it is a command list run at every hit.
- `//` and `/*` are the console's `comadd` and `commit`. A comment's text is never evaluated, and a `comadd` typed here is not saved or listed by the comment tools.
- A comparison is never an assignment: `print {d1==7fff}` is a read. An assignment is looked for outside quoted strings only.
- An assignment to a debugger temporary variable is not a write, but `temp0=w@100=1` is: the chain reaches memory.
- A line of several commands is split at each `;` outside brackets and quotes, and each command is classified alone.

A line that assigns the temporary variable of a `control`, an address counted beside a run's target, names that control in `note`. The write moves the `hits_since_armed` that `declaration_list(kind="breakpoint")` reports, not a run's `control_hits`. Writing -1 makes the control stop the machine at its next hit.

MAME drops a packet longer than its debugger connection takes, without answering, and the wait that followed would blame the wrong thing. The same limit covers every tool that sends a console command: a long `condition`, a `find` pattern, a `memdump` path.

A parse error, such as `unknown command` or `unbalanced quotes`, stops the line there: the commands after it never ran, and a `g` behind it leaves the machine stopped. An error printed while a command ran, such as `Error in expression` or `Error opening file`, leaves the rest running.

A command refused while it ran still counts as a write, because the console evaluates parameters in order: `print d0=5,zzz` writes D0 before it refuses `zzz`. An error the answer cannot pin on one command names the whole line. Only the error shapes the console is known to print are matched, each at the start of a line.
A bare comparison typed as a command, `print d1==1234`, is an assignment expression to the console's parser and is refused; in braces it answers.

A `statesave` or `stateload` typed here is completed as [`state_write`](states.md#state_write) completes its own when MAME holds it, and `note` says so. MAME keeps one held save or load at a time, so a line that held several completes only the last.

comment_list.what: List every saved comment, or one cpu's, each with its address and whether MAME's disassembly shows it.
comment_list.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset, right after the comment of the entry below was added.
comment_list.ask: Which comments are saved for this game?
comment_list.reads: One comment is saved, and `truncated` is `false`: the reply lists every one. No cpu was named, so the rows are every cpu's.

arguments.cpu: Lists this cpu's comments only. Left empty, every cpu's.

returns.comments: The comments this reply shows. Each row has `ref`, `text`, `addr` once resolved, `state`, and `why` when it is not shown.
returns.comments_total: How many comments are saved, listed or not.
returns.truncated: `true` when there are more comments than the reply lists. `comment_write(method="save")` writes them all.
returns.declarations: The saved breakpoints file the comments live in: its `path`, and `persistent`, `false` when they last only this session.

refuses: A cpu the machine does not have (`unknown_ref`).
why: It reads the saved comments and asks the machine nothing, so it answers while the program runs.
MAME also ties a comment to a checksum of the instruction bytes under it. Code that moves in RAM hides its comment in MAME's disassembly, while the comment stays saved.
why_more: What `state` says of a comment:

- `armed`: MAME's disassembly shows it.
- `unarmable`: saved but not shown. `why` says the reason.
- `unresolved`: its symbol is not in this build.
- `stale`: a raw address saved over another build.

- Each row also carries `by`, `cpu`, `created_at`, `origin`, `inherited` and `age_s`, as a saved breakpoint's row does.
- A rebuild can bring several comments to one address. All are kept: MAME's disassembly shows the first it can, and each other reads `unarmable`.
- A field with nothing to give is an object: `available` is `false` and `why` says the reason, as `cpu` when none was named.
- While the machine runs the reply adds `last_stop`.

comment_write.what: Change the saved comments: add or delete one, or save them all to a file and load them back.
comment_write.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset with the example session's symbol file loaded, which names the coin routine `count_coin`.
comment_write.ask: Leave a note on the coin routine: a coin increments the credits, then the BCD copy.

call.text: a coin: INC credits, then the BCD copy

comment_write.reads: The comment is saved on `count_coin`, which is `0xb583` on the main cpu, in a file that outlasts the session. Nothing was there before, so `replaced_comments` is empty.

head: method
what it does
rows: Puts `text` on `ref`. A comment already there is replaced.
Writes every comment to the file `dest`.
Reads the comment file at `path` into the saved comments, all or nothing.

arguments.ref: For `add` and `delete`: a symbol or a `0x` address.
arguments.text: For `add`: one printable line, at most 237 UTF-8 bytes.
arguments.cpu: For `add` and `delete`: the cpu whose code is commented. Left empty, the one the debugger is showing.
arguments.dest: For `save`: the file to write, an absolute or `~`-led path. A comment file already there is replaced; any other file is refused.
arguments.path: For `load`: the comment file to read, an absolute path.

returns.comment: `add`: the comment as saved, a row as `comment_list` gives it.
returns.replaced_comments: `add` and `load`: the comments whose text was replaced, as they were.
returns.dropped_comments: `save`: comments only the replaced file held, each by `ref` and `cpu`. They are gone from the file.
returns.added: `load`: how many comments are new. `unchanged` counts those already saved with the same text, `parsed` the rows read.
returns.held_in_memory: `true` when the saved breakpoints file could not be written: the change lasts until `close`.

refuses: An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
`add`, `delete` or `load` while the program runs (`not_stopped`).
A `ref` that is a pointer, an expression or a `seg:off`, or a `text` that is empty, too long or not one printable line (`bad_argument`).
Bare hex that names no symbol, or a `delete` whose `ref` matches no comment (`unknown_ref`).
A `dest` that is the saved breakpoints file itself, a link, or a file that is not a comment file (`bad_argument`).
A `load` file with a bad row or a cpu the machine lacks: nothing is loaded (`bad_argument`).
A saved breakpoints file that cannot be written: the change is kept in memory (`host_failed`).
why: The change is saved first, and MAME's disassembly is fed after. If the session breaks in between, the message says so, and the next `start` feeds the saved comments again.
One address shows one comment. An `add` where one exists replaces its text and keeps its `ref`, so a comment made by symbol keeps following its symbol.
`save` and `load` are how a project keeps its comments under version control beside its symbol file. `load` is all or nothing, and the file wins where both comment an address.
why_more:
- A comment's `state` is `armed` once MAME's disassembly shows it. `unresolved` names a symbol this build lacks: the comment stays saved and is shown once a build has it.
- The file has no build column, so a raw address loaded into another build is trusted. Comment by symbol what must survive a rebuild.
- A rebuild can bring several comments to one address. An `add`, `delete` or `load` there reaches the one whose `ref` it spells, else the one MAME's disassembly shows.
- A `stale` comment made the other way, by symbol where yours is by address or the reverse, is reached only by its own spelling.
- `save`'s `dest` is in a folder that exists, and its path holds no comma, semicolon, quote, space, bracket or control character.
- MAME's console cannot carry a text holding `"` or ending in `\`: it is saved and reads `unarmable`. If it replaces one that was shown, the old text is cleared.
- A `delete` over instruction bytes that changed since leaves MAME holding the old text, hidden, until `close`.
- A file with two comments a rebuild put at one address loads both, so what `save` writes of them reads back.
- MAME writes its own comment files into a folder inside the session's temporary folder, so nothing deleted here comes back from them.
- `comments_total`, `dropped_total` and `replaced_total` count the whole lists; `truncated` says a list was cut. `declarations` names the saved breakpoints file, as in `comment_list`.

- The file `save` writes is UTF-8 with no byte order mark, and its lines end in LF.
- Line 1 is exactly `# comments v1: ref<TAB>cpu<TAB>created_at<TAB>text`, and each row after it holds those four columns.
- Rows are sorted by cpu, then by ref, so a diff shows only what changed.
- `cpu` is the cpu's absolute tag, and `created_at` reads `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS+00:00`.

input.what: Press one of the board's inputs by name (a coin, a start button), hold it for some frames and let go.
input.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped about seven seconds after power-on. The example session drops this coin as the first step of a `perform`.
input.ask: Drop a coin into the first slot and keep it pressed for four frames.
input.reads: Bit 0 of the port went low while pressed (`0xcf` to `0xce`), from frame 419 to frame 423. `active` confirms the port showed the press; whether the game counted the coin is for its memory to say.

arguments.port: The input port that has the field, as MAME names it: `:P1`.
arguments.field: The field of that port to press, as MAME names it: `Coin 1`.
arguments.value: What the field is set to: non-zero presses a digital field, an analog one takes a value in its range. Left out, 1; a string is a `0x` number.
arguments.frames: How many frames the field stays pressed: one or more. Left out, 4.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the whole call, in real seconds, up to 600. Left out, 30.

returns.released: `true` when the field was let go. `false` when another stop cut the run first: the field is still pressed, and `frame_release_planned` is the frame that lets it go.
returns.active: Whether the port showed the press, read back as the field was let go. `false` means the press never reached the port.
returns.frame_set: The frame at which the field was pressed; `frame_released` is the frame at which it was let go.
returns.port_before: The port's value before the press. `port_held` is its value while pressed, and `mask` the field's bits in it.
returns.verdict: How the run of frames ended: `ELAPSED` when every frame asked ran, `OTHER_STOP` when a breakpoint or a watch stopped it first.
returns.pending: `true` when the script got no answer: the press has not happened, and may still happen when the console next runs a line.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
An empty `port` or `field`, or `frames` below 1 (`bad_argument`).
A port the machine does not have, or a field that port does not have (`unknown_ref`).
A machine with no screen, a vector display for one: the press is timed by counting frames (`no_channel`).
More than 8 lines still waiting in the console (`bad_argument`).
A script the console ran twice, which pressed the field twice, so the reply would describe neither press (`console_rerun`).
A script that ran and logged no press: the field was not shown pressed (`readback_refused`).
A time limit that ran out before the frames ran (`wait_expired`).
A run that was not confirmed stopped: the field may still be pressed (`not_settled`).
A console that died before it ran the script (`reader_died`).
why: An arcade board has no keyboard. Its coin slots, buttons and switches are named fields of input ports, so pressing a field by name works on any board.
A game that detects the edge of a press needs the field let go between two presses: two coins are two calls.
A press is play, not a write. It leaves `altered`, the mark that this session has written to the machine, as it was.
why_more: `seconds` covers the whole call: every run of frames and every wait for the console takes what is left of it.
Only one press waits at a time. A new `input` first lets go of a field an earlier call left pressed.
Before its own line the call steps the machine once for each line still waiting in the console (`lines_ahead`, `drain_steps`). The console's other counts are described under [`lua`](#lua).

`route` says which way the press went in: always `ioport` here, MAME's input ports. `name`, `player` and `defvalue` are what MAME says of the field: its name, its player and its value when not pressed.
The reply ends with what every stop returns, described in [Running and stopping](../../REFERENCE.md#running-and-stopping).

lua.what: Run a Lua script inside MAME, with all of MAME's Lua interface, and get back what it prints.
lua.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped anywhere. The example session asks this late in a game.
lua.ask: Ask MAME itself which machine this is, with one line of Lua that only reads.
lua.reads: The script printed `Gridlee`, and only what it prints comes back. `evaluated_by` says the console needed one step of the machine to run the line, which is why the program counter moved on from `pc_before`.

arguments.script: The Lua to run: one chunk of at most 16000 characters. Only what it `print`s comes back; a `return` value does not.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the console's answer, in real seconds, up to 600. Left out, 5.
arguments.read_only: `true` says the script only reads, and nothing checks it. Left out, the session is marked `altered`: written to by this session.

returns.output: What the script printed. Past 4000 characters it is cut: `clipped` is `true` and `output_path` names a file with all `output_chars` of it.
returns.evaluated_by: How the console came to run the script: `one step`, or more steps when other lines were waiting ahead of it.
returns.pc_before: The program counter before the step that ran the script; `pc` is where the machine stopped after it.
returns.lines_ahead: How many lines were waiting in the console before this one. The machine was stepped once for each.
returns.console_reruns: How many earlier scripts the console ran a second time during this call. One that wrote has written twice.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
An empty script, or one over 16000 characters (`bad_argument`).
More than 8 lines still waiting in the console: `run_for` one frame runs them (`bad_argument`).
A script that fails to compile or raises, with the console's own `error:` text (`bad_argument`).
No answer within `seconds`; a late answer shows in `log`, on the `process` log (`wait_expired`).
A console that died before it ran the script; with `pending: true` the script may still run later (`reader_died`).
why: The other tools check what they did: `input`, `throttle`, `record`, `state_write`. `lua` is for what none of them does, and it promises less: nothing checks what the script changed, so the session is marked `altered` unless you say `read_only`.

The console runs a line only when the machine moves, so the call steps the machine once. The script reads the machine after the instruction at the stop has run. With lines waiting ahead it steps once for each, and the script reads the state after the last step.

The whole script is one chunk: a `local` on line 1 is seen on line 2, and a script that fails says so in the console's own words. Guard any callback you install with `pcall`, because its error does not come back to the call that installed it.
why_more: A callback's error goes elsewhere. A write tap's goes nowhere, and the tap keeps firing. A frame notifier's or a periodic callback's is a `[LUA ERROR]` line per call in `log`.
MAME's console is a plugin. `start` refuses a MAME that does not have it, before anything is launched.
`call` is the line that closes this call's output in the `process` log. When `seconds` runs out, the refusal says how many steps were taken, and a late answer shows in `log`, ending with that line.

MAME reads the console on a thread its own source calls unsafe: a step at the wrong moment can make it run the previous script again, or drop a line. Every reply that reads the console counts what happened:

- `lines_ahead`: lines waiting before this call's own. `drain_steps` or `evaluated_by` says how they were run first.
- `reader_steps`: extra steps given because the console had not picked the line up.
- `resent`: the console took the line and never ran it, so it was sent again. A second time is refused `reader_died`.
- `thread_errors`: how many times the console's reading thread died.
- `console_reruns`: earlier scripts run a second time. `altered` alone cannot say a write happened twice.
- `thread_errors`, `console_reruns` and `resent` are on every reply that read a script's answer back, zero included.
- Session totals sit under `session.console`. They grow when a call reads its answer back and once more at `close`, so a `throttle` asked while stopped adds none till then.

The tools that send a script of the server's own carry the same counts: `input`, `throttle`, `record`, `audio_record`, `screen_signature`, `screen_map_find` and `screen_map_write` with `method="add"`. [`debug`](write.md#debug) does not use this console: it talks to MAME's debugger.
A script of the server's own that raises is refused by its error. A port or field the machine lacks is `unknown_ref`, a recording with no screen `no_channel`, anything else `unexpected_answer`.

throttle.what: Choose whether the machine runs at real speed or as fast as the host can.
throttle.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at reset before anything has run. The example session then runs the game five seconds.
throttle.ask: Turn real-speed throttling off so the game fast-forwards, then confirm the switch was applied.

then.lead: Then, once the game has run, look for the tag in MAME's log:

throttle.reads: `pending` means the switch waits for the machine to move, and `tag` is the text it writes to MAME's log once applied. The second call finds that line, `throttled=false`: `TARGET` means the pattern matched.

arguments.on: `true` runs the machine at real speed; `false` fast-forwards it, as fast as the host can.
arguments.seconds: With the machine running, how long to wait for the switch to be confirmed, in real seconds, up to 600. Left out, 5.

returns.pending: `true` when the switch is not applied yet: the machine is stopped, and the console runs the line when it next moves. `false` once applied.
returns.tag: The text the switch writes in MAME's log when it applies, `MAME_MCP_THROTTLE#n`. Give it to `log_wait` on the `emulator` log to wait for it.
returns.frame: The frame at which the switch applied, and `waited_s` how long that took. Only when `pending` is `false`.
returns.applies: For a switch not applied yet, when it takes effect; `confirmed_by` says which later replies confirm it.

refuses: A switch not confirmed within `seconds` on a running machine: it is still waiting, and `status` lists it (`wait_expired`).
A machine that reports the other setting after the switch (`readback_refused`).
why: The switch is a line sent to MAME's console, and the console runs a line only when the machine moves. Asked on a stopped machine it cannot wait for its own confirmation, because nothing runs the line while it waits. The reply is `pending`, with the `tag` to look for.

So, stopped at a breakpoint, ask and then `resume`: the machine runs at the new speed from its first frame. A switch not applied yet is looked for again at the next stop, by `status` and by `close`. Until then `status` lists it in `throttles_pending`.

A switch that never took effect is not forgotten. When the console went past the line without applying it, or the machine reports the other setting, every later reply says so in `session.throttles_not_applied`, which stays set until `close`. Asking again fixes the speed and the record stays: this session measured at a speed nobody chose.
why_more: No call is refused over a switch that was not applied. The record is on every reply because the call that would report it is one nobody has to make. Until the console has gone past the line there is no record: the `pending` you were given is still true.

The console reads a line on a step, on the next frame emulated, or after a debugger command on a MAME build that refreshes after one. A machine that stops again before its next frame leaves the switch waiting.

The `tag` is text to search the log for, never a `mark`, which is a position in a log. Its number counts every line this session sent to the console, not the switches. `log_wait` takes a regular expression, so `#1` also matches `#10`.
`start`'s `throttle_from_frame` is the same switch decided at launch: fast-forward up to that frame, real speed after it.
`tagged_lines`, on a refusal, are the log lines that carry the tag.

state_list.what: List the session's saved states, with the size of each and where it was saved.
state_list.ask: Which saved states does this session have?
state_list.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, after a state was saved as `two_credits`. The example session gives `start` a `state_dir` of its own.
state_list.reads: The summary counts one state, and `state_dir` is the folder it is in: `sta/gridlee` under the `state_dir` given to `start`.

returns.state_dir: The folder the states are in: `sta/<system>` under the `state_dir` given to `start`, or under the session's temporary folder, which `close` deletes.
returns.states: One row per `.sta` file: `name`, `path`, `bytes`, and the `frame` and `pc` it was saved at. A value not read is unavailable, with `why`.

why: The list is read from the folder, not from the machine, so it answers while the program runs.
`frame` and `pc` are known only for a state this session saved. A `.sta` from an earlier session has them unavailable, as a `load` of it reports.

A `.sta` that is no regular file (a link to nothing, a directory, a FIFO) has `bytes` unavailable too, its `why` saying what is there. So has one under a name no `load` reads, such as `Boss_1.sta` where a state is `boss-1`: its `why` says to rename it.

state_write.what: Save the emulated machine to a file under a name, or load a saved one back.
state_write.ask: Save the machine here under the name two_credits, so I can come back to it.
state_write.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped after two coins went in. The example session then plays on to the level card before it loads the state back.

then.lead: Later, with the game on its level card, the load:

state_write.reads: The name is kept as `two-credits`, saved at frame 543. The load puts the machine back at that frame: `verified` says it reads as it did at the save, and `rom_check` that the ROM still matches.

head: method
what it does
rows: Writes the machine to a new file. It never overwrites one.
Replaces the machine with a saved one. Every later reply then carries `altered`: this session has written to the machine.

arguments.name: The state's name, spelled as a file name is: `Boss_1` becomes `boss-1`. At most 64 characters, with at least one letter or digit.

returns.path: The state's file: `<name>.sta` in the state folder.
returns.frame: The frame the machine is at. On `save` it is the frame the file holds, kept with `pc` to check a later `load`.
returns.verified: On `load`: `true` when the machine reads as it did at the save. Unavailable, saying why, when nothing could prove the load.
returns.saved: On `load`: the `frame` and `pc` the save recorded. Unavailable for a state this session did not save.
returns.rom_check: On `load`: `OK` when the ROM still matches the `reference_rom` given to `start`. Unavailable when the session has none.
returns.held: Set when MAME held the save or load for a pending timer: one instruction was stepped to complete it, and this says where the machine stopped.

refuses: A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A name with no letter or digit, or longer than 64 characters (`bad_argument`).
A `save` under a name that already has a file (`bad_argument`).
A `load` of a name with no state, or whose `.sta` is no regular file (`unknown_ref`).
A `save` that leaves no file, a file that is not a MAME state, or a state of another machine, which `system` names (`readback_refused`).
A `load` after which the ROM no longer matches, or the machine does not read as saved: `differs` gives the `cpu`, the `register`, and its `saved` and `loaded` values (`readback_refused`).
A save or load MAME still holds after one instruction: it would land inside the next run (`not_settled`).
why: MAME's console refuses a bad state in silence: a damaged file and another machine's state both come back as attempted, with nothing in the log. So the file's header is checked before the console sees it, and after a load the machine is compared with what the save recorded.
`verified` is `true` only when that comparison could tell a load from no load. For a state this session did not save, or a machine that already read as saved, it is unavailable and says why.

MAME can also hold a save or a load instead of running it, when a timer is pending on the stopped machine. Left alone it would run inside your next run, so the tool steps one instruction to complete it and says so in `held`.
why_more: Both methods use the debugger console's `statesave` and `stateload`, which work on a stopped machine. MAME is started with `-statename %g`, so the file is in `sta/<system>` whatever an ini file says.

A stopped machine gets a pending timer when a memory write runs a driver handler that synchronizes. On a MAME build that redraws the screen after a console command, a redraw that raises an input line does it too. Nothing can end the one step early: while a save or load is pending, MAME stops at no breakpoint or watchpoint.
A held save's `frame`, `pc` and registers are read after that step, so they are the file's, and `stop_seq` numbers the stop the step made.
MAME's emulated clock runs on across a load: it does not go back with the state.

A recording repeats from one saved state only on a driver whose game logic does not run while the screen is drawn. Logic run from the screen update depends on when the screen was last drawn, which a state does not hold, so `load` then `record` can give two different recordings. Compare such recordings against a tolerance.

`mark` is where each log ended as the load was sent, one position for `emulator` and one for `process`. `log` and `log_wait` take it as `since_mark` to read what came after. It is a position in the file, not a moment, so a line written before the load and not yet flushed lands after it.

A load is a stop of its own, with the readings every stop returns, described on the [Run](run.md) page. Its `errorlog` is the lines MAME's log gained (`lines_total`, `truncated`, `lines`, `mark`), not what the `log` tool reads. `taps_across` lists each count or capture that was running across the load, as [`reset`](write.md#reset) does.

series_capture.what: Save chosen frames of the screen as PNGs beside a manifest, for `image_compare` to read.

arguments.at_frames: The frames to keep, as an ascending list of frame numbers. Give this or `first` and `last`, never both.
arguments.first: The first frame of an evenly spaced range, given with `last`.
arguments.last: The last frame of the range. A series holds at most 1000 frames.
arguments.step: The spacing of the range: every `step`-th frame from `first`. Left out, 1.
arguments.crop: The rectangle of the screen each PNG holds, `[x, y, width, height]`. Left out, the whole screen.
arguments.dest: A new folder for the series, absolute or starting with `~`, which outlives `close`. Left empty, a folder in the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the run, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 60.

returns.manifest: The path of the series' manifest, `manifest.json`; the PNGs sit beside it, named by frame as `f000123.png`.
returns.count: How many frames were written; `first` and `last` are their lowest and highest numbers.
returns.distinct: How many different pictures the series holds. One means nothing changed on screen.
returns.kept_after_close: `true` when the series is in a `dest` you named, `false` when `close` deletes it.
returns.lost: Frames asked for that the emulator skipped drawing, as `[first, last]` ranges. They have no picture and are left out.
returns.verdict: How the run ended, as `run_for` reports it: `ELAPSED` when every frame ran.

refuses: Both `at_frames` and a range, or neither; a list that is not ascending; more than 1000 frames (`bad_argument`).
A frame that is not ahead of the frame the machine is at (`bad_argument`).
A `crop` that leaves the screen, or a `dest` that exists (`bad_argument`).
An `at_frames` list too long for one console line: give `first`, `last` and `step` (`bad_argument`).
A run another stop ends before the last frame is read: no series is written from part of one (`cut_by_other_stop`).
A run in which every frame asked for was skipped (`no_progress`).
A machine with no screen (`no_channel`), or one that is running (`not_stopped`).
why: Frame numbers are the emulated frame counter, the one `run_for(frames=)` counts, and every frame asked for must still be ahead. The call runs the program to two frames past the last one and stops there.
Each picture is MAME's own rendering of its frame, in the colours the palette held at the frame's end, read one frame later. A frame the emulator skipped drawing is listed in `lost`, never filled in.

A series frame is always an RGB PNG, because a series is for comparing what the screen showed. `gfx_film` may write the same frame as an indexed PNG, so their checksums never match: compare the two with `image_compare(method="image")`.
why_more: The reply is also a stop: it carries `verdict` and the fields `run_for` returns, with the readings taken at each stop.
`frames_asked` is how many frames the call named, and `frame_source` says what the numbers count: `frame_number`, the emulated frame counter.
series_capture.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped at frame 553, as a game begins. The frames asked for must be ahead of the frame the machine is at.
series_capture.ask: Keep every eighth frame from 557 to 581 as pictures in a folder named series.
series_capture.reads: Four frames between 557 and 581 were kept, three of them different pictures, and none was lost. `ELAPSED` means the run reached its end: the machine went from frame 553 to 583.

record.what: Record an exact number of frames of the screen to an AVI video, then stop the program again.

arguments.frames: How many emulated frames to record: 2 or more.
arguments.dest: An absolute `.avi` path that does not exist yet. Left empty, the file goes to the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the whole call, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 60.

returns.path: The AVI, once the reply has read it back as a finished file.
returns.avi_frames: How many frames the file's own header says it holds.
returns.ended: `true` once the recording is closed. `false` when a stop cut the run short: it stays open until the machine reaches `frame_end_planned`.
returns.began: `false` when a stop came before the first frame: the recording begins at `frame_begin_planned`.
returns.verdict: How the run ended, as `run_for` reports it: `ELAPSED` when every frame ran, `TIMEOUT` when `seconds` ran out first.
returns.view: The MAME view the video was drawn through, chosen at `start`.

refuses: `frames` under 2, or a `dest` that is not a new `.avi` path (`bad_argument`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A machine with no screen or no frame counter (`no_channel`).
A file that does not read back as a finished AVI with frames in it (`readback_refused`).
A script that answered and logged no mark, not even the line it writes as it is evaluated (`readback_refused`).
A script MAME's console ran twice, which begins two recordings on one file (`console_rerun`).
A run that did not come to a stop within `seconds` and could not be ended (`not_settled`).
why: The recording is counted in emulated frames, so no time of your clock goes into the file. A script inside MAME begins and ends it as frames are drawn, and it cannot end a recording on the frame that begins it: one frame is refused.

A stop that is not the time limit, such as a breakpoint, cuts the run short and leaves the recording open or not begun. It goes on when the machine reaches the planned frame, unless the next `record` call cancels it.
When `seconds` runs out first, the recording is closed there and the reply reads the file back: `ended: true`, with the frames it ran.
why_more: Lines already waiting in MAME's console are run before the script is sent, one instruction each, so the frames asked for are the recording's own.
The reply is also a stop: it carries `verdict` and the fields `run_for` returns, with the readings taken at each stop. `frame_before` and `frame_after` say how far the machine moved.
A reply with `pending: true` means the console had not run the script when the call ended, so nothing is known about the recording yet.

- The script proves each step by a mark in MAME's `error.log`, carrying this call's own number, so a stale mark is never taken for a later call's.
- A frame notifier that fails leaves no mark, so the reply says `began: false` or `ended: false`, never a finished empty file.
- `frame_begin_planned` is predicted from the frame counter as the script is evaluated, one frame later inside a vertical blank.
- A refusal after the run began says how far the machine moved, in `frame_before` and `frame_after`.
- A `not_settled` run leaves out the recording's fields, and its message says whether the frame notifier may still be armed.
record.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped on the card that announces a level, right after START is pressed with two credits.
record.ask: Record the next 30 frames of the screen to a video named card.avi.
record.reads: The video holds 30 frames, 562 to 591, and the recording is closed (`ended`). `ELAPSED` means every frame ran, and `native` is the MAME view the video was drawn through.

audio_record.what: Record an exact number of frames of sound to a WAV file, then stop the program again.

arguments.frames: How many emulated frames of sound to record: 2 or more.
arguments.dest: An absolute path that does not exist yet. Left empty, the file goes to the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.
arguments.seconds: The time limit of the whole call, in seconds of your clock. Left out, 60.

returns.path: The WAV, once it has been checked.
returns.samples: How many samples the file holds, at `sample_rate_hz` a second, for each of its `channels`.
returns.emulated_s: The emulated time the recording spans, in seconds.
returns.sample_min: The lowest sample value in the file, beside `sample_max`. The two equal mean a constant level: silence.
returns.ended: `true` once the recording is closed. `false` when a stop cut the run short: it stays open until the machine reaches `frame_end_planned`.
returns.verdict: How the run ended, as `run_for` reports it: `ELAPSED` when every frame ran, `TIMEOUT` when `seconds` ran out first.

refuses: `frames` under 2, or a `dest` that exists (`bad_argument`).
A machine that is running (`not_stopped`).
A machine with no screen or no frame counter (`no_channel`).
A stretch with no mixer update, a machine with no speaker, or a mixer already recording (`readback_refused`).
A WAV whose header, length or sample count does not agree with the run (`readback_refused`).
A script that answered and logged no mark, not even the line it writes as it is evaluated (`readback_refused`).
A script MAME's console ran twice (`console_rerun`).
why: The recording spans exactly `frames` frame periods of emulated time. MAME's mixer writes in updates of a fiftieth of an emulated second. So the sound begins up to one update before the first frame and ends up to one before the last.

The file is checked before its path is given, because MAME's writer checks none of its writes and fills the header's two sizes only at close. The header must agree with the file, and the samples with the stretch, within one update.
Silence is reported, never refused: it is a fact about the program. A constant level is silence to the ear whether it is zero or not.
why_more: Two is the fewest `frames` that always hold a mixer update on a screen under 100 Hz.

A stop that cuts the run short leaves the recording open or not begun, as [`record`](#record) explains. An open recording gains nothing while the machine stands at the debugger, since no mixer update runs there.
Its marks in `error.log`, its planned frames and its refusals after the run began follow [`record`](#record)'s rules.
audio_record.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped on the card that announces a level. The free set lacks Gridlee's sound samples, so the game is silent here.
audio_record.ask: Record the sound of the next 30 frames to a file named card.wav.
audio_record.reads: The file holds 24000 samples for about half an emulated second. `sample_min` and `sample_max` are both 0: the recording is silent, because Gridlee's sound samples are not in the free set.

snapshot.what: Save a still of the screen as it is now to a PNG file.

arguments.dest: A new path for the PNG, absolute or starting with `~`, in a folder that exists. Left empty, the session's temporary folder, deleted at `close`.

returns.path: The PNG, checked to be complete.
returns.sha256: The file's SHA-256: the value a line of reference checksums holds for `image_compare(method="golden")`.
returns.view: The MAME view the still was drawn through, chosen at `start`.

refuses: A `dest` that exists, is relative, or sits in a folder that does not exist (`bad_argument`).
A `dest` holding a comma, semicolon, quote, space, bracket or control character (`bad_argument`).
A PNG that is not complete on disk in time (`unexpected_answer`).
why: The still is MAME's own snapshot, and it works while the program runs. To capture a finished picture and not one half drawn, `run_to` the address where the drawing routine ends, then take the snapshot.

MAME's `snap` command treats even an absolute path as relative to its snapshot folder, so the tool takes the still under its own name and moves the file. MAME's command line cannot carry the characters refused in `dest`.
A `dest` is checked before MAME is asked, so a refused path costs no snapshot.
snapshot.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped while the card that announces a level is on screen.
snapshot.ask: Save a picture of the screen as it is now to card.png.
snapshot.reads: The still is a complete PNG at `path`. `native` is the MAME view it was drawn through.

captures.what: List the files this session's tools wrote, each read again now: whether it is still there, its size, what it holds.

returns.captures: One row per file: `kind`, `path`, `present` and `bytes`. An AVI adds `avi_frames`; a WAV adds `samples`, `channels` and `sample_rate_hz`.

why: Every file is read again at each call, so the list says what is on disk now, and it answers while the program runs. A file deleted since stays listed, with `present: false`.

`kind` is the file's extension (`avi`, `wav`, `png`, `trace`), or `image` for a picture a graphics tool or a series wrote. An AVI's or a WAV's counts are unavailable once the file no longer reads as finished.

The file of addresses a `trace` writes beside its trace is not listed. Neither is an unfinished recording: a recording its call answered still open or not begun is not listed, since that call's reply holds its path.
captures.on: On Gridlee, a free ROM from mamedev.org, near the end of a session that has recorded a video, a sound and a trace and saved pictures.
captures.ask: List the files this session has written so far.
captures.reads: Fifteen files: a video, a snapshot (`png`), a sound file, a trace and eleven pictures (`image`) that the graphics tools and the series wrote.

image_compare.what: Compare two pictures, two series of frames, or one region across a series, and get the difference as numbers.

head: method
what it compares
rows: Two PNGs, pixel by pixel: how many pixels differ, and where.
Two series, frame by frame: how many frames are equal, and the first that differs.
One rectangle across a series: the frames at which it changes.
A series or a folder of PNGs against a file of reference checksums.

arguments.a: The first PNG for `image`, or the first manifest for `series`. An absolute path, or one starting with `~`.
arguments.b: The second PNG or manifest, compared with `a`.
arguments.crop: The rectangle to compare, `[x, y, width, height]`, for every method but `golden`. Left out, the whole picture.
arguments.shift: For `image`: `[dx, dy]`, how far `b` is moved before the two are compared. Left out, no move.
arguments.tolerance: For `image`: the difference in one colour component still counted as equal, 0 to 255. Left out, 0.
arguments.manifest: For `region` and `golden`: the series to read, by the path of its manifest.
arguments.measure: For `region`, what is followed: the rectangle's `signature`, its `changed_pixels` since the frame before, or its `match` with `ref`. Left out, `signature`.
arguments.ref: For the measure `match`: the PNG, of the crop's size, the rectangle is compared with.
arguments.threshold: For `match`: the fraction of the rectangle's pixels that must equal `ref`, above 0 and at most 1. Left out, 0.98.
arguments.limit: For `region` and `golden`: how many items each list shows, 1 to 1000. Left out, 40; the whole count is beside the list.
arguments.dir: For `golden`: a folder of PNGs to check, in place of `manifest`.
arguments.checksums: For `golden`: the file of reference checksums, in the format `shasum -a 256` writes.

returns.differing_pixels: For `image`: how many pixels differ by more than `tolerance`. Zero means the two are equal over the rectangle compared.
returns.bbox: For `image`: the rectangle that holds every differing pixel, `[x, y, width, height]` in the coordinates of `a`.
returns.first_differing: For `series`: the first frame that differs, with its `frame` number, its `differing_pixels` and its `bbox`.
returns.differing: For `series`: how many paired frames differ. For `golden`: the names of the files whose checksum differs.
returns.transitions: For `region`: each change as `[frame, value]`, the first `limit` of them; `transitions_total` counts them all.
returns.path: For `region`: a JSON file written beside the manifest, with every transition and each frame's value.

refuses: An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
Two pictures of different sizes with no `crop` that lies inside both (`bad_argument`).
A `crop` that leaves the picture, or a `shift` that moves it wholly off itself (`bad_argument`).
A path that is relative or missing, or a file that is no PNG or no `scry-series/1` manifest (`bad_argument`).
A manifest with a frame changed since it was written, or a row edited by hand (`bad_argument`).
A series that never changes, two series with no frame number in common, a region that never changes, or checksums that name no file examined (`control_silent`).
why: `image` compares the colours two pictures show, so an indexed PNG and an RGB one of the same screen are equal. `golden` compares file bytes through their checksums, so those two files differ.
Two pictures of different sizes are refused unless a `crop` lies inside both. A tool that shows a picture enlarges it by its `scale`, so take both at `scale=1` before comparing them.
A `crop` that leaves the picture is refused, never padded: a padded crop would compare pixels nobody drew.
why_more:
- `series` pairs frames by number. Frames only one series has come back in `only_in_a` and `only_in_b` as `[first, last]` ranges.
- `region` answers `start`, the first frame and its value, then the transitions. `gaps` counts the frames between one transition and the next.
- `golden` pairs files and checksum lines by file name. `matched` counts the equal ones, `missing` lists lines with no file, `extra` files with no line.
- The reply repeats the arguments it took, each path in full. For `image`, `a` and `b` come back with the file's `path` and `sha256`.
image_compare.on: On two frames of the series the Gridlee example of [`series_capture`](captures.md#series_capture) wrote, frames 557 and 581. No machine is running.
image_compare.ask: How different are frames 557 and 581 of the series?
image_compare.reads: 8975 pixels differ between the two 256x240 pictures, all inside the rectangle `bbox`: 242 wide and 213 high, from (4, 17). A `tolerance` of 0 counts any difference.

audio_compare.what: Measure a WAV recording, or compare two, and get loudness, silence, timing and closeness as numbers.

head: method
what it answers
rows: One recording: how loud it is, whether it is silent, when the sound begins and whether it clips.
Two recordings: whether they are equal and, if not, how close they are.

arguments.path: For `measure`: the WAV to measure, 8- or 16-bit PCM. An absolute path, or one starting with `~`.
arguments.b: For `diff`: the reference recording, of the same sample rate, `channels` and bit depth as `a`.
arguments.window: The part of the recording to read, `[from_s, to_s]` in seconds. Left out, the whole file.
arguments.channel: For `measure`: which of the file's `channels` to measure, numbered from 0. Left out, each of them.
arguments.align: For `diff`: `true` lines up where the two sounds begin before comparing them; `false` compares from the first sample. Left out, `true`.

returns.measures: For `measure`: one row for each of the `channels`, with `channel`, `peak_dbfs`, `rms_dbfs`, `silent`, `silence_spans` (its `count` and `first`), `onset_s`, `clipping_run` and `clipped`.
returns.pcm_sha256: For `measure`: the SHA-256 of the samples in the window, equal for two files that hold the same sound.
returns.exact: For `diff`: `true` when the two windows hold the same bytes.
returns.class: For `diff`, the verdict in one word: `exact`, `inaudible`, `audible` or `different`.
returns.snr_db: For `diff`: the signal-to-noise ratio of `a` against `b`, the worst of the `channels`. Unavailable when the two are equal once lined up.
returns.aligned_by_samples: For `diff`: how many samples `a` was moved to line up with `b`.

refuses: An argument the method does not take (`bad_argument`).
A file that is not 8- or 16-bit PCM, holds no sample or cannot be read (`bad_argument`).
A `window` outside the recording, or a `channel` number the file does not have (`bad_argument`).
For `diff`, two recordings that differ in sample rate, `channels` or bit depth (`bad_argument`).
For `diff`, two recordings that are both silent over the window (`control_silent`).
why: The sound itself never comes back, only numbers, so a client that cannot listen checks a recording through them.
Each of the `channels` is measured and compared on its own, never mixed down first. Mixed, one in antiphase would cancel, and two swapped ones would average to the same sound.

`diff` lines up the two sounds unless `align` is `false`, so a recording that starts a few samples later is not called different. With `align` `false`, two recordings made from the same stop are compared sample for sample.
why_more:
- A steady level that is not zero is no sound: loudness, silence and the comparison read the window less its mean.
- Two recordings whose lengths are more than a tenth of a second apart are `different`.
- The reply repeats `path`, `a`, `b` and the `window` it read.
audio_compare.on: On the WAV the Gridlee example of [`audio_record`](captures.md#audio_record) wrote. No machine is running.
audio_compare.ask: Did card.wav record any sound? Measure it.
audio_compare.reads: The summary's `ch0` is the first and only one of the file's `channels`, and it is silent over its half second. Gridlee's sound samples are not in the free set, hence the silence.

perform.what: Run a list of this server's tools in one call, in order, stopping at the first step that fails.
perform.ask: Drop a second coin, let the game run two seconds, then keep only the scanned bytes that now hold 2.
perform.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped with one coin in and a `scan` of the first 2 KB open.
perform.reads: All three steps ran and none failed, so `failed_at` only says why it holds no number. `held` is 0 because no step carried `recorded` values to give again.

arguments.steps: The list to run: each step is `{"op": <tool>, ...}` with that tool's own arguments. Give this or `path`, never both.
arguments.path: A saved step list to replay in place of `steps`: a file under `.scry/perform/` or one `perform_export` wrote. Absolute, or starting with `~`.
arguments.settle_seconds: How long each wait for the program to stop may take, before a step that needs it stopped. 0 never waits; left out, 30 seconds.
arguments.summaries: `true` cuts each step's reply but the last to a short row and writes the full replies to a file. Left out, every reply comes back whole.
arguments.until_frame: A frame number: the list repeats until a stop reads that frame. Needs `summaries` and a `run_for` step; left at 0, the list runs once.

returns.ran: One row per step that ran: its `op`, its `reply` and the `cpu` that reply names. With `summaries` a row adds its `step`, and `ran_path` and `replies_path` hold them all.
returns.held: How many steps carried `recorded`, the values a replayed step must give again, and gave them. 0 when no step carried any.
returns.failed_at: The step that failed, counted from 0, with its `op` and `reply` in `failed`. When none failed it is `available: false` with a `why`.
returns.errors: Every step refused before anything ran, each with its `step`, `op`, `code` and `message`.
returns.verdict: Comes once the list waited for a stop: `TARGET` with the stop in `stopped`, or `TIMEOUT` with a `note`. A list that waited for none says `still_running`.
returns.stops: With `summaries`, the server's own count of the stops: `stop_seq_first`, `stop_seq_last`, `surveyed` (how many a reply described), `by_cause` and `unaccounted`.

refuses: A step that names no tool, an argument its tool does not take or a value it refuses. Nothing runs, and `operations` lists the tools a step may name (`bad_argument`).
A step's `cpu` the machine does not have, or a bare hex `ref` that names no symbol, also before anything runs (`unknown_ref`).
Both `steps` and `path`, neither, or an empty list (`bad_argument`).
A step that answers INVALID: the list ends there (`step_failed`).
A step whose reply differs from its `recorded` values; the reply names the `field`, the `recorded` value and what it `got` (`diverged`).
A step that needs the program stopped while it still runs and `settle_seconds` is 0 (`not_stopped`).
`until_frame` without `summaries`, without a `run_for` step, or at a frame the program has already reached (`bad_argument`).
`until_frame` on a machine with no screen device, which has no frame to count (`no_channel`).
A stop that reads no frame under `until_frame`, since nothing then says whether the frame came (`unexpected_answer`).
The emulator gone before a step could run (`session_broken`).
why: The whole list is checked before its first step runs, so a refusal never arrives after earlier steps changed the machine. What only a running step can know refuses at that step: a symbol against the table loaded by then, a file an earlier step writes.

A step that needs the program stopped waits up to `settle_seconds` for the stop. A wait that runs out ends the list `TIMEOUT`: the steps after it were built on what it waited for. So does a step whose own wait missed, a `log_wait` or `screen_wait` that timed out.

A step may carry `recorded`, a `{field: value}` object of its own reply, and a reply with other values ends the list. That turns a list into a test, and `perform_export` writes such lists from a session.
why_more: `until_frame` counts what happens before a frame when nobody can know how many steps that takes. Every stop a watch makes takes a step without moving the frame, so a list sized by guessing ends short, with a smaller count that looks right.

The call ends right after the first step whose stop reads the frame, even mid-list, and `frame_reached` says which. It needs a `run_for` step because `run_for` carries on past a watch's stop, where `run_to` and `step` end at the first.
On a running program the first stop starts the count. Running out of steps or seconds is a `TIMEOUT` that names the last frame read.
Every pass compares each step with its `recorded` values again, so a stop recorded on the first pass diverges on the second. A document `perform_export` writes carries no `until_frame`.

With `summaries`, `steps_total` counts the rows and `truncated` says the reply shows fewer. Read `stops` for a count and `ran_path` for the whole table: a count made by hand from cut rows comes out wrong and looks right.

On a machine with several cpus the list leaves the visible cpu, the one the debugger shows, as it found it. At its end, failed or not, it puts back the cpu visible before the first step, or the one the last `cpu_focus` step chose, running nothing. Once the program runs, the next stop decides.
`visible_cpu` is that cpu after the list, and `visible_cpu_kept` tells how it was kept: `before`, `asked`, `after`, `restored`, `moved_to`, and a `why` when it was not put back.

drive.what: Send an input as a list of steps, then check the program reacted by waiting for a new line in the log.
drive.ask: Drop a coin and check the game counted it: wait for its coin counter line in the log.
drive.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, stopped in its attract mode five seconds after power-on.
drive.reads: The summary says a new log line matched `expect` after the coin went in. The line itself is under `verify` in the whole reply, with the lines `looked` kept.

arguments.act: The steps to run, in the shape `perform` takes: `{"op": <tool>, ...}`. Required, and never empty.
arguments.expect: A regular expression: the log line that shows the program reacted, waited for after the steps. Left out, nothing is checked and `verify` says `checked: false`.
arguments.seconds: How long to wait for the `expect` line. Left out, 5 seconds; given without `expect`, the call is refused.
arguments.pattern: A regular expression that picks which new log lines `looked` shows. It changes nothing in the check; left out, every line.
arguments.limit: How many of those lines `looked` shows, the newest: 1 to 400. Left out, 40.
arguments.settle_seconds: As in `perform`. With `expect`, the last step's stop is not waited for: waiting for the line is the wait.
arguments.summaries: As in `perform`: `true` cuts each step's reply but the last to a short row.

returns.act: What the steps did, in the fields of a `perform` reply: `ran`, `steps_completed`, `failed_at` and the rest.
returns.verify: The check: `checked` says whether one ran and `seen` whether the line came, with the `line`, the `verdict` (`TARGET` or `TIMEOUT`) and `waited_s`.
returns.looked: Under `emulator`, the newest `lines` written since the steps began that match `pattern`, with `lines_total` and `truncated`.

refuses: `seconds` without `expect`, or an empty `act` (`bad_argument`).
A bad step or argument in `act`, before anything runs; `operations` lists the tools a step may name (`bad_argument`).
A step's `cpu` the machine does not have, answered with its `cpu_tags` (`unknown_ref`).
A step that answers INVALID (`step_failed`).
The program stopped at the debugger without the line: a stopped program logs nothing more, so waiting would not help (`wait_stopped`).
A refusal of the steps themselves comes back with its own code, such as `not_stopped`, `session_broken` or `diverged`.
why: The log is marked once, before the first step, so a line written before the input is never taken for a reaction.

An arcade board has no debug port to write to, so the line is looked for in the emulator log: what MAME's driver and this server's scripts write with `logerror`. A driver that logs a lot fills it fast, so keep `pattern` narrow.
The reply holds no picture of the screen: `snapshot` takes one, and `screen_signature` gives a number for it. With no line to wait for, `perform` is the call to make.
why_more: `verify` also carries `expected`, `lines_before` and `lines_total`, and a `why` when no line came or nothing was checked. If the steps ran out their own wait, nothing is checked and it says `available: false`. `looked.emulator` adds `lines_written`, `since_mark` and `pattern`; `act` adds, with `summaries`, `steps_total`, `truncated`, `ran_path`, `replies_path` and `stops`.

perform_export.what: Write the session's calls since `start` as a script that replays them and checks their answers, with no model.
perform_export.ask: Save what we did in this session as a script that replays and checks it without you.
perform_export.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, in a session that dropped two coins and read the credits.
perform_export.reads: Nine calls replay, three of them as checks, and 14 calls were left out. `cut` is unavailable because nothing ended the script early; `kept` says the script is now a candidate for `promote`.

arguments.dest: The `.json` file to write, required: absolute, or starting with `~`. Refused when it exists, unless `overwrite`.
arguments.overwrite: `true` replaces a `dest` that is already there. Left out, an existing file is refused.

returns.steps: How many calls the script replays; `path` is the file written.
returns.checks: How many of them compare a reading with its `recorded` values, the answer the session got.
returns.dropped: The last 40 calls left out (reads the script does not check, refused calls, calls that change nothing), each with its `call`, `op` and `why`; `dropped_total` counts all.
returns.cut: The call the script ends before, with its `call`, `op` and `why`. It is `available: false` when every call a replay can run was kept.
returns.replay: The command that [replays the script](../../REFERENCE.md#from-a-session-to-a-test-that-replays-itself), run from this server's repository. It exits 0 when every step gave its `recorded` values again.
returns.kept: Says the script was saved as a candidate for `promote`: it reads "N saved for `promote`", and names a repository that has no `.scry/` folder yet.

refuses: A `dest` that does not end in `.json`, is a directory, or exists without `overwrite` (`bad_argument`).
No `start` that succeeded, one that was cancelled, or no call left that a replay could run (`no_recording`).
why: The script keeps the calls that move the program and a few readings as checks, each with the answer it got as `recorded`. A call that left the program at a new stop is checked on that stop's `pc` and `frame`.

The script ends at the first call no replay can reach. A `resume`, or a run that the clock or a `stop` ended, stops the cpu at a point inside its frame that no replayed run reaches. Every later stop would inherit the shift.

So move with `run_for`, `run_to` and `step`, which stop at the same point on every run, and keep `resume` for the end. Leave the `dest` of a step that writes a file empty: a file the session named is still there on replay, and the step is refused.
why_more: When the frames are known, `cut` says how many the run took, and a `run_for` of that many replays it up to that frame's start. The script also ends at a call with no reply, a refusal after the program moved, and a program found elsewhere than the call before left it.

A `debug` line is replayed and its printed answer never checked; one that moved the program is checked on its stop. An `image_compare(method="golden")` over files that dropped calls wrote is dropped too.
A reader that steps the program to read is kept as a step. How far a Lua reader steps follows the host's clock, so on a rare run it lands elsewhere and the replay says so at that step.

The script carries `start`'s arguments as given, host paths included; the replay's `--binary` and `--rompath` replace them. `needs.states` lists the saved states it loads and does not save, checked before anything plays. `needs.declarations` lists the breakpoints, watches and registerpoints saved when the recorded `start` began, which a replay must find again.

promote.what: Review what the session learned and write the entries you approve into the repository's `.scry/` folder.
promote.ask: Show me what this session would save into this folder's `.scry/`, without writing anything.
promote.on: On [Gridlee](../../demos/gridlee/README.md), a free ROM from mamedev.org, late in a session that started the game, added a screen map and exported a script. `root` names a folder with no `.scry/` yet.
promote.reads: A review writes nothing: `total_bytes` is the size of its candidates, and `store_bytes` what the folder would hold with them and its two own files. `would_create` lists what a first approval adds.

arguments.dry_run: `true` reviews: it lists every candidate and writes nothing. It cannot be given together with `entries`.
arguments.entries: The entries to write, each `<kind>/<name>` with a kind of `start`, `maps` or `perform`. Only these are written.
arguments.names: A new name for an entry as it is written, as `{"<kind>/<name>": "<new name>"}`. Left out, each keeps its name.
arguments.root: The repository whose `.scry/` folder takes every entry of the call: absolute, or starting with `~`. Left out, each entry goes to its own repository.

returns.candidates: A review's list. Each `entry` has its `kind`, `name`, `file`, `bytes` and `change` (`new` or `update`), an update its `diff`, and one from another repository says `from`.
returns.unchanged: A review's entries that already equal their file in `.scry/`, so there is nothing to approve.
returns.unwritable: Entries this call cannot write, each with its `reason`: most often a repository with no `.scry/` folder, which a call with `root` creates.
returns.written: An approval's entries as written, in the fields `candidates` uses.
returns.draft: After an approval, the session's candidates not yet written to `.scry/`.
returns.would_create: What an approval would create that is not there yet: `.scry/`, its `about.json` and its `README.md`. An approval names what it created in `created`.

refuses: Nothing saved yet: no `start`, screen map or exported script of this session is a complete candidate (`needs_call`).
Both `dry_run` and `entries`, or neither (`bad_argument`).
An entry the session did not save, one named twice, or a name in `names` for an entry not in `entries` (`bad_argument`).
Without `root`: no entry with a `.scry/` folder to go to, or entries of two repositories in one call (`bad_argument`).
A name two repositories saved, unless `root` is one of them (`bad_argument`).
Two entries that `names` would write to one file (`bad_argument`).
An entry a review lists as `unwritable` (`bad_argument`).
More entries of one kind, or more bytes, than a `.scry/` folder may hold (`bad_argument`).
A `root` that is relative, is no directory, or names the `.scry/` folder itself (`bad_argument`).
A file the host would not write; the message names what was written before it (`host_failed`).
why: Nothing is written into a repository until a call names the entries to write. The `.scry/` folder is tracked, so every entry is reviewed before it is written, and only an approved call creates the folder. [The `.scry/` folder](../../REFERENCE.md#the-scry-folder) says what it holds.

`dry_run=true` lists each candidate that would change the folder: its file, its size and whether it is new or an update, an update with what changes. It names the candidates that would change nothing, and what an approval would create beside the entries.

An entry belongs to one repository, fixed when it is saved: the one a call read it from, else the one whose profile the current `start` read. A `start` that read no profile names none: no argument says where a program's repository is, and `rompath` is often a folder many programs share. Its entries are written only where `root` says.
why_more: A candidate is saved only when complete: a start profile with the arguments it cannot start without, a screen map its reader parses, a script with a check. A reply that saves one also names each repository with no `.scry/` folder and the `root` to give.

An entry a call loaded (`start(profile=)`, `screen_map_write(method="load")`, `perform(path=)`) gives its name to what is learned next, so saving it again is an update. An update keeps the keys that belong to a run as the file has them.

Every path in an entry is written as a placeholder ([the rule](https://github.com/scry-mcp/scry-core/blob/main/docs/store-paths.md)), so the tracked file reads the same on any machine. `close` names in `draft` what was left unwritten, and the candidates stay until the server ends.

`store` is the `.scry/` folder the call reads or writes, `store_bytes` its size with the entries written, and `total_bytes` the size of the candidates listed. A `diff` holds `added`, `removed` and `changed`, each change with its `path`, `was` and `now`; `changed_total` counts them when the list is cut.

knowledge_find.what: Ask what a number is called on this machine and what its documentation says it does: a vector, a chip register, an input, a device.
knowledge_find.on: Needs no session and no program: the base answers from its own copy, for any chip it holds.
knowledge_find.ask: What do registers 8 to 10 of the AY-3-8910 do, and does MAME follow the manual?
knowledge_find.reads: One entry matches, so it comes whole: the manual's rows first, with MAME's verdict where it gave one, then MAME's own notes. Each row cites its lines, and `sources` links each document once.

arguments.id: An entry's id, as another reply cites it, such as `ay8910:register:0x07`: that entry whole. `<id>#<n>`, such as `ay8910:register:0x07#1`, answers its row `n`, with a link to each line.
arguments.kind: What the number is: `vector`, `call`, `error`, `port`, `irq`, `memory`, `input`, `device`, `register` or `command`. Left empty, every kind.
arguments.key: The number as a reply prints it, or a range such as `0x3C0..0x3CF`; for an `input`, `:IN1/Coin 1`.
arguments.text: Words looked for in names, aliases and the rows' text. A word ending in `*` matches by prefix.
arguments.device: A chip's key, or a tag of the running machine such as `:ymsnd`: everything that belongs to it.
arguments.scope: A chip or a cpu: `ay8910`, `pic8259`. Left empty, the session's cpus and chips; with no session, all.
arguments.limit: How many entries are listed: 1 to 50. Left out, 10.

returns.entries: Rows with `id`, `kind`, `key`, `name`, and `live: true` on the machine's own. One match or an `id` answers whole: `rows`, the document's first with `verdicts`, then MAME's notes.
returns.examined: How many entries were searched, so a zero says what it is a zero of.
returns.nearest: When nothing matched: the entries next to the number or the words.
returns.note: When nothing matched: that the number stays a number.

refuses: None of `id`, `kind`, `key`, `text`, `device` (`bad_argument`).
A `key` that is no number or range of that `kind`, or a `scope` the server does not hold (`bad_argument`).
An `id`, a row `<id>#<n>` or a `device` the base does not hold (`unknown_ref`).
A kind read from the machine with no session (`no_session`).
why: An entry says what the chip's or the cpu's documentation says, and MAME's code where it differs, with the lines each row was read from. The base is the server's own copy: it answers while the program runs.
What the machine says about itself (inputs, devices, the memory map) was read at `start` and is never asked of MAME again, so it cannot slow a call.
